title: Steinitz – Meitner, Vienna 1882
solution: George Mackenzie – Wilhelm Steinitz, Vienna 1882 34.Be4! The only drawing move, and easy to find, as Black’s mate threat means White has no other sensible try. 34. Rg1?? loses to everything, but is mated most swiftly by 34... Qxg2+!. 34...Qxe4 Obviously not 34...Rxe4?? 35.Qf8 mate. 35.Bf6+ Bxf6 36.Qxf6+ ½–½ White has a perpetual on f6 and f7. The Woodpecker Method Wilhelm Steinitz A win by an unsound combination, however showy, fills me with artistic horror. 225

title: Hartlaub – Lasker, Germany 1908
solution: Carl Hartlaub – Emanuel Lasker, Germany 1908 7.Nxe5! A surprisingly common theme in Lasker’s games. 7...d5 7...fxe5 8.Qh5+ g6 (8... Ke7 9.Qxe5 mate) 9.Qxe5+ Qe7 10.Qxh8+– 8.Qh5+ Or just as good is: 8.Re1 fxe5 9.Rxe5+ Kd7 10.Bg5!+– 8...g6 One source gives this game as played in New York 1911, with 8...Ke7 9.Nf7? Qe8? 0–1 (??) as the final moves, none of which makes any sense. 9.Nxg6 hxg6 10.Qxh8 Or 10.Re1+ first. 10...dxc4 There are many ways to win and you don’t have to decide in advance. Easiest is: 11.Re1+ Kf7 12.Bh6+–

title: Capablanca – Watson, Schenectady 1909
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – C.E. Watson, Schenectady 1909 White has a minor piece less, but can more than make up for it with the following double threat: 30.Rf6! Nxf6 31.Rxf6 Qh5 32.Bd1 Not necessary, but a luxury White can afford. 32.Nxe6 and 32.Rxe6 are also winning. 32...Qe8 33.Rxe6+– Black is an exchange up, but since he has no chance against all the pawns and an invasion on the kingside, he resigned now.

title: Capablanca – Malowan, New York (simul) 1922
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – W . Malowan, New York (simul) 1922 36.Nxf7+?! looks like a combination and was played in the game, but Black had 36...Rxf7 37.g6 Rxf5+! 38.Rxf5 Rg7 when he collects the g-pawn with a draw. title: Ribli – Spassky, Montpellier 1985
solution: Zoltan Ribli – Boris Spassky, Montpellier 1985 85...Qxh6+! 85...Qd2+ is the complicated way to draw (zero points). The queen endgame with g- and h-pawns is generally drawn with the defending king in front of the pawns. It surprised the whole Swedish team when we learned this at the 2016 Olympiad in Baku. However, 85...Qd2+ should lose in a practical game. First, Black has to find 86.Qf4 Qd8+ 87.Qf6+ Kh7! 88.Qxd8 with stalemate. 86.Kxh6 ½–½ Stalemate! 86.Kf5 keeps the game going, but it’s an easy draw anyway.

title: Steinitz – Anderssen, London 1862
solution: Wilhelm Steinitz – Adolf Anderssen, London 1862 33...e3! Black had a dominant position and an extra pawn, so he could win slowly in many ways, but this is the quickest winner. 34.f3 Or 34.fxe3 Rg6 quickly forces mate. 34...Rg6 It’s still a forced mate. 35.g4 fxg4 36.f4 Bd5 37.Nd4 Ra6 Pretty, but an even faster mate was possible with the prosaic 37... Rg2+. 38.Rxa6 Rb1+ 0–1 White resigned, rather than allow a mate such as: 39.Kh2 Rh1+ 40.Kg3 Rg1+ 41.Kh2 Rg2+ 42.Kh1 Rg3+ 43.Kh2 Rh3+ 44.Kg1 Rh1 mate

title: Steinitz – Bird, London 1870
solution: Wilhelm Steinitz – Henry Bird, London 1870 White is a pawn down, so has to create something. 19.Nge6! fxe6 It would have been better for Black to give up the exchange on f8 with 19...g6². With a pawn and opposite-coloured bishops for the exchange, Black has some compensation. Note that the bishop on b5 is essential after 19...g5 20.Nxf8 gxf4 21.Nd7!. Now, 21...Bd8 22.e5! is the only winning move, but that’s not necessary to see before sacrificing the knight. The point is 22...a6 23.exd6+ Kxd6 24.Ne5!+– threatening a fork on f7. 20.Ng6+ Kf7 The knight would not escape from h8 after 20... Kf6, but White has 21.Nxf8+– . 21.Nxh8+ Kf6 The knight looks trapped, but it has two ways to escape. 22.f4 22.Re3 is also good: 22...g5 23. Rf3+ Kg7 24.Rxf8 Kxf8 25.dxe6± with a safe square on f7. 22...Ne7 23.e5+!+– Kf5 24.Bd3+! 1–0 Not only can the white knight escape, the black king is mated!

title: Steinitz – Dufresne, Liverpool 1874
solution: Wilhelm Steinitz – Jean Dufresne, Liverpool 1874 If only Black had time for 24...b6 and 25... Kb7 – it’s not going to happen. 24.d5+! Kb6 24...Qxd5 25.Be4 wins the queen and 24... Kxd5 is not a nice move to play. There are many ways to stop the king from returning to “safety”, and the fastest is 25. Qh1+ Kc5 26.Be3+ Bd4 27.Bxd4 mate. 24... Kd7 is not the direction the king wants to go. However, Black threatens to shut out White’s rook with 25...Be5. Best is 25.Re6!+– when White continues with 26.f6 or 26.Bb5+. 25.Be3+ 25.Re4 also wins. Black’s king can’t go to c7 after 25...c5 26.Bd8++–. 25...c5 26.Qd8+! The only winning move. 26...Qc7 27.Qxg8+– And White won. 27.Bg5 or 27.Qe8 should also win.

title: Steinitz – Martinez, Philadelphia (1) 1882
solution: Wilhelm Steinitz – Dion Martinez, Philadelphia (1) 1882 10...Nxd4!³ White loses the queen no matter which way he recaptures. 11.Bxf4 Steinitz played the unchallenging 11.c3. Also no help is 11. Qxd4 Bc5–+ or 11.Nxd4 Qxd1–+ . 11...gxf4 11...Nxf3?! 12.Qd5!³ creates a pin along the fifth rank and wins back the piece. 12.Nxd4 Black did not win any material (he was a pawn up in the diagram), but destroying White’s centre is an achievement. 12...Qh4+ 12...Qxd1 13.Rxd1³ is also good. However, due to White’s exposed king and undeveloped rook on h1, it’s more logical to keep on the queens. 13.Kg1 Bc5³ Black continues with ...Ne7 or ...Nf6 and ...0–0.

White undermines the defence of the rook on e6 while simultaneously defending e1, and doesn’t have to worry unduly about the check on f1. 25...Rxf7 26.Qxe6 26.Rd8+± is about as strong. 26...Rf1+ 27.Be1 Qb6 28.Qxb6?!± On account of Black’s open king, White should have kept the queens on the board with: 28. Qe2+– 28...axb6 29.Kd2 Kg8 30.Rd8+ Bf8 31.Rd7?! Better is 31.Bg3 with a winning position. 31...Bd6 32.Ke2? Rg1 33.Kf2 Rh1 34.Ke2 Rg1 ½–½

title: Steinitz – Chigorin, Havana (4) 1892
solution: Wilhelm Steinitz – Mikhail Chigorin, Havana (4) 1892 23.Rxd4! Steinitz keeps the dark-squared bishop, and can always attack on the dark squares with Bxe6 and a few heavy pieces on the h-file. The position is winning, and the end came quickly in the game. Instead 23.Bxd4+? Nxd4 24.Rxd4 is about even. 23...Nxd4 24.Rxh7+ Forcing mate, but not obligatory to see since the alternative is easy enough: 24.Bxd4+ Rf6 and White is winning if the queen hurries towards h6 with a threat along the way. There are three ways: a) 25.Qb5 Ref8 26.Qg5+–, b) 25.Qd3 and c) 25.Qd1. 24...Kxh7 25.Qh1+ Kg7 26.Bh6+ Or 26.Qh6+ Kf6 27.Qh4+ Kg7 28.Bh6+ Kh8 29.Bxf8 mate, or 29.Bg5+ Kg7 30.Qh6 mate. 26...Kf6 27.Qh4+ Ke5 28.Qxd4+ Or 28.Qg3+ Ke4 29.Qe3+ Kf5 30.Qf4 mate. When the queen took on d4, Chigorin resigned instead of allowing 28...Kf5 29.g4 mate or 29.Qf4 mate. The Woodpecker Method 251

There are three ways: a) 25.Qb5 Ref8 26.Qg5+–, b) 25.Qd3 and c) 25.Qd1. 24...Kxh7 25.Qh1+ Kg7 26.Bh6+ Or 26.Qh6+ Kf6 27.Qh4+ Kg7 28.Bh6+ Kh8 29.Bxf8 mate, or 29.Bg5+ Kg7 30.Qh6 mate. 26...Kf6 27.Qh4+ Ke5 28.Qxd4+ Or 28.Qg3+ Ke4 29.Qe3+ Kf5 30.Qf4 mate. When the queen took on d4, Chigorin resigned instead of allowing 28...Kf5 29.g4 mate or 29.Qf4 mate. The Woodpecker Method 251

title: City of Liverpool – Steinitz, corr. 1893
solution: City of Liverpool – Wilhelm Steinitz, corr. 1893 20...Rxd5! 20...Nd4?! 21.Be7! is a nice resource, with the point that White can take back twice on e7 with check – thus not giving Black time to capture on h5. Black has to play: 21...hxg6 22.fxg6 Qxe7! (not 22...Bxg6?! 23.Qxg6 Rxe7 24.Nxf6++– or 22...Rxe7?! 23.Qh7+ Kf8 24.Nxf6+–) 23.Nxe7+ Rxe7 Black is not losing, but probably worse and certainly not winning as in the game. 21.exd5 Nd4 22.Ne7+ There is no defence against 22...Nxf5 23.Rxf5 hxg6 winning material. 22...Qxe7 It’s over, which White soon accepted.

title: Lasker – Steinitz, Moscow (2) 1896
solution: Emanuel Lasker – Wilhelm Steinitz, Moscow (2) 1896 35.Nec5+! 35.Nbc5+ is the same and 35. Nxd6 also wins, but only if White finds: 35... Kxd6 36.Bf4+ Kd5 (36...Kd7 37.Nc5+ Ke8 38.Bd6!+–) 37.Re5+ Kc4 38.Nc5! White threatens mate- in-three with 39.Rc1+ and the try 38...b4 39.b3+! Kb5 40.Rxe7! Bxe7 41.Rxe7! is hopeless (full points if you saw this far). White wins back the exchange after 41...Rb6 42.Bc7. White also has a winning position after 35.Bf4 Nf5 36.Nbc5+ Kc7 37.Na6+. 35...dxc5 36.Nxc5+ Kd6 37.Bf4+ 37.Bxe7+ is also winning and good enough for full points. title: Steinitz – Blackburne, Vienna 1898

R3g4³ and Black wins the bishop thanks to the mate on h4 if the rook protects the bishop. 37...Rh3 There is no perpetual or anything else compensating for the pawns after: 37...Kxc6 38.Re6+ Kc5 39.Rxh6 Rg2+ 40.Ke3+– 38.Bd5+– With a lot of luck, Blackburne held half a point in a long endgame (½–½, 93 moves).

title: Lasker – Blackburne, London 1899
solution: Emanuel Lasker – Joseph Blackburne, London 1899 31...Rh1+! 31...Bxg3? 32.Nxg3 Qh4 33.fxg4 Qxg3 threatens 34...Rh2 35.Qe2 Qh4 with mate, but 34.Re3³ keeps the disadvantage to a minimum, as does 34.Qf3³. 32.Kxh1 Bxg3! 33.Nxg3 33.Re2 and Black has two ways: a) Qh4+ 34.Kg1 Bh2+ (or 34...Nf2–+) 35.Kh1 Nf2+ 36.Rxf2 Bg3+ 37.Kg1 Bxf2 mate b) 33...Nf2+ 34.Kg1 (34.Rxf2 Qh4+ 35.Kg1 Bxf2 mate) 34...Nxd1 With an easily winning position. 33...Nf2+ 34.Kg1 Nxd1–+ White only gets a rook for the queen; there is no way to catch the knight on d1 without losing another piece.

title: Lasker – Sterling, Paris 1900
solution: Emanuel Lasker – Manuel Marquez Sterling, Paris 1900 12.f5! The pawn sacrifice is good enough even on just positional grounds, but there is also a tactical follow-up. 12...gxf5 13.Bh6! 13.Ne7 Qxa4 14.Nxf5 Rg8! 15.Nxg7+ Rxg7 16.Qxf6 Qxc2 gives some counterplay, although Black should not have enough for the piece after 17.Nc3 Qxg2 18.Rf1±. 13...0–0 13...Bxh6 14.Qxf6 is a winning double attack and 13...bxc6 14.Bxg7+– was the game (1–0, 28 moves). 14.Qg3 Other moves are interesting as well, so full points if you have seen any of the other lines instead: 14.Bg5 Ne4 15.Ne7+ is winning, as is 14.Bxg7 Kxg7 15.g4!. Even the immediate 14.g4 seems to give White a winning position. 14...Ne8 15.Ne7+! Qxe7 16.Bxe8 f6+– White exchanged the “dead” knight on c6 for Black’s knight and is a piece up.

title: Lasker – Chalupetzky, corr. 1903
solution: Emanuel Lasker – Ferenc Chalupetzky, corr. 1903 13.Bxc6+? bxc6 14.Qxc6+ Kf7 15.Qxa8 wins an exchange, but White loses: 15...exd4+ 16.Kf2 Bb7 and 17... Qe4–+. The exercise was a red herring! If he captures on c6, White has to limit the damage with 15.Qd5+! Kg6 16.0–0!µ with two pawns for the piece. But the best move is: 13.Be2! T o avoid the check on h5, Black should exchange queens with 13...exd4 14.Qxd4 Qb4+ 15.Qxb4 Bxb4+ 16.c3 when White has a slight advantage with fewer pawn islands. Other non-blundering 13th moves also give full points.

title: Capablanca – Dus-Khotimirsky, St Petersburg 1913
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – Fedor Duz-Khotimirsky, St Petersburg 1913 28.Nf5! fxe6 28...gxf5 29.Qxf5 with unavoidable mate. Instead, the best defensive try is 28...Kh8 29.Qe4! (several other moves provide a clear advantage) 29...fxe6 30.Nxe7 Qxe7 31.dxe6 Nc3 32.Qxd4+ Qg7, but White is winning all the same. 29.dxe6! Qc7 29...Qxf3 30.Nxe7+ wins a piece, but there is no tactical way to finish the game after 29...Rb8. However, there is no need for it; White is winning if he avoids the queen exchange. 30.Qc6! Not obligatory, but a precise move that wins the b-pawn (1–0, 47 moves). 30.Qg4/g3 and 30.Nxe7+ are also decent enough.

title: Capablanca – Stahr, Chicago 1915
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – J.M. Stahr, Chicago 1915 33.Rxe6+! 33.Qxf5+ exf5 34.Rxc7 Rxg2+ is probably winning for White, but he only keeps one of his pawns. title: Capablanca – Wolff, New York 1915
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – Christoph Wolff, New York 1915 22...Rxe3! 23.fxe3 Bxe3+ If Black does not keep on the queens, White can safely continue with the counterplay on the queenside without fearing an attack: 23...Qxe3+?! 24.Qxe3 Bxe3+ 25.Kf1 Bxc1 26.Na4 Ba3 27.Ra5 And White’s active pieces compensate for the material deficit. 24.Kh1 Bxc1 Black has won two pawns, but Capablanca could have taken one back with 25.Nxd5! cxd5 26.Rxc1µ when White has drawing chances.

title: Capablanca – Shipley, Philadelphia (simul) 1918
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – Walter Shipley, Philadelphia (simul) 1918 32...Nxa3+! 33.Rxa3 33.bxa3 Qxc3! and White dearly misses his b-pawn. 33...Rxb2+! The game continued 33...Bxa3? 34.Nxb5! Qxb5² when Black was a pawn up, but Capablanca showed that the h-pawn is worth more than that. 34.Qxb2 Bxa3 35.Qb3 Rxh6µ Now Black is two pawns up, although White has some counter-chances due to Black’s misplaced rook. title: Capablanca – Kostic, Havana (3) 1919

Bxb7+. 27...Qb6+– The point is 27...Qxe5 28.Bxb7+ Kb8 29.Nc6++– with a fork. 28.Nxb7? Easier was 28.Bxb7+ Kb8 29.Nc6+ Kxb7 30.Nxd8+ with too many pieces for the queen, and a decisive attack. 28...c4! solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – C.H. Reid, London 1928 17...Rxh4+! The move order 17...Bxg2 works as well, as 18.Nxg2 loses to 18...h4. But 17...Rhg8 18.Bh3! is not as clear, although probably still winning after 18...f5. 18.gxh4 Bxg2 19.Kxg2 19.fxe5 was the hopeless game continuation: 19... Qh3+ 20.Kg1 Bxf1 and White resigned. 19...Qg4+ 20.Kf2 Qxh4+ 20...Nd4 21.Bxd4 Qxf4+ also wins. 21.Kf3 White has to give up several pieces to avoid mate after for example: 21...Nd4+ 22.Ke4 f5+ 23.Kd5 Qf6–+

title: Capablanca – GS Pharmacy, New York (simul) 1931
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – Gracie Square Pharmacy Chess Club, New York (simul) 1931 37.f6+! Black has to take on f6 to defend the g6-pawn. 37...Rfxf6 38.Nh5+ Kh7? No better is 38...Kh8 39.Qh6+ Kg8 40.Qg7 mate . Black had to play 38... Kf7 39.Rxf6+ Rxf6 40.Qxf6+ Ke8. Without rooks, he threatens both 41...bxa2 and a lot of checks. The trick is to take on g6, defend the f1-square and the e4-pawn with check, and then take on b3: 41.Qxg6+ Kd8 42.Qf6+ Kc7 43.Qf4+ Kb7 44.axb3+– 39.Nxf6+ White can take care of the black counter- threats in more than one way, for instance: 39...Kg7 40.Nh5+ Kh7 41.Qe7+ Kh6 42.Ng3+– The knight moves back to g3.

title: Capablanca – Thomas, Hastings 1934
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – George Thomas, Hastings 1934 24...Qa5–+ A double threat against the bishop and knight. Thomas started with 24...Rxd2?! 25.Rxd2 before playing 25...Qa5. He was winning, and won, but there was little reason to give away the exchange. Perhaps he feared the knight coming to d6, but apart from giving up the exchange when that happens, he could also win with: 25.N c4 Rxd1! 26.Rxd1 26.Nxa5 Rxe1+ 27.Bf1 Ba6–+ 26...Qxb5 27.Nd6 Qd7 When all is well and safe.

title: Capablanca – Lilienthal, Moscow 1936
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – Andor Lilienthal, Moscow 1936 35.Nxb7! Rxb7 35...Nxc4! is the best defence. White is a pawn up after 36.Bxc6+± but there is work left to do to convert. 36.Bxc6+ Rd7+– It is possible to imagine a situation where Black blockades the queenside pawns, but it is not realistic with careful play. The best defence was 14...g6, since Black gets the bishop pair if White takes the exchange. But 15.Ng7! puts an end to that dream. 15.Bxg7! An important move – otherwise 14.Bh6 makes no sense. 15...Nxg7 16.Qh6+–

title: Euwe – Spielmann, Bad Pistyan 1922
solution: Max Euwe – Rudolf Spielmann, Bad Pistyan 1922 24...Rxf4! 25.Kxf4 25.Rxf4 Qe1+ 26.Rf2 26...f4+–+ followed by 27... Qxf2 (or 26... Ne5 with a winning attack). 25...Ne5–+ A double threat: 26...Nxd3 and 26...Ng6+. (There is also nothing wrong with 25...Qe4+ 26.Kg5 Qxd3–+ or 25...Qd6+ 26.Kg5 f6+!–+ winning a rook.) Solutions to Intermediate Exercises Max Euwe Let us repeat once more the methods by which we can increase our combinative skill: (1) by careful examination of the different types and by a clear understanding of their motives and their premises, (2) By memorising a number of outstanding as well as of common examples and solutions, (3) Frequent repetition (in thought, if possible) of important combinations, so as to develop the imagination. Strategy & Tactics in Chess (1937) 276

title: Euwe – Sonnenburg, Amsterdam 1927
solution: Max Euwe – Sonnenburg, Amsterdam 1927 9.Nxf7! Kxf7 10.Qf3+ The king does not want to go to the e-file, but the alternatives are even worse. 10...Ke7 a) 10...Kg6 11.Bd3+ Bf5 12.Qxf5 mate; b) 10... Kg8 11.Rxe6! Qxe6 12.Qxd5 (mating), or 12. Bxd5 (winning). 11.Bxd5 White has a huge advantage due to the exposed black king, but it is not easily winning. The best line for both seems to be 11...Ne5 12.Qh5 Qxd5 13.Rxe5 Qc6+– when White should develop a piece and then adjust his attacking ideas depending on Black’s reply.

title: Colle – Euwe, Amsterdam (1) 1928
solution: Edgard Colle – Max Euwe, Amsterdam (1) 1928 26.Rxf7! Re8± White is satisfied to restore material equality. Both players have passed pawns, but only White has active heavy pieces, attacking the queenside pawns. White should not trade off his active rook as he did in the game (0–1, 35 moves) and instead either push the e-pawn (best) or take the b-pawn either immediately or after the intermediate 27.Qe7. Instead 26...Rxf7 27.Qc8+ is mate.

title: Felderhof – Euwe, The Hague/Leiden/Scheveningen 1933
solution: William Felderhof – Max Euwe, The Hague/Leiden/Scheveningen 1933 White has dangerous threats against the uncastled black king, so Black gives up a piece to get to safety, and then continue with his own attack. 16...Ba3! 17.bxa3 The best move. In the game, White was too kind with 17.Qa4?, as there was no reason to allow Black to keep the piece with 17...Bxb2+–. Also bad is 17.Rxd7? Bxb2+! 18.Bxb2 Qxb2+–+ when White does not win anything on d7, since his king will obstruct the d-file. 17...0–0!µ Black has a promising attack with threats such as ...Rfc8 and ...Qxa3+.

title: Euwe – Tylor, Nottingham 1936
solution: Max Euwe – Theodore Tylor, Nottingham 1936 17.Rxc5! As simple as it looks; the bishop on e7 is pinned. But 17. Bc2?! Qe6 18.Bf5 Qd6!± does not win a pawn. 17...Bxg5 White won smoothly after: 17... Bxc5 18.Bxd8± (1–0, 25 moves) 18.Nxg5! 18.Rc7± is also a pawn up. 18...Qe7 A double threat, but there are many remedies. We will give the easiest solution for a human as the main line and three alternatives. 19.Bxd5 a) 19.Qh5 h6 20.Qxf7+ Qxf7 21.Nxf7 Kxf7 22.Rc7+ Rd7 23.Rxb7 Rxb7 24.Bxd5+ Kf6 25.Bxb7+– with three extra pawns. b) 19.Qc2 Qxg5 20.Bxd5 Bxd5 21.Rcxd5+– and Black loses due to the back-rank problems. c) 19. Nxf7 and White continues with a capture on d5, after which the rook on a8 is in trouble. 19... Kxf7 (19...Qxf7 20.Rdxd5! Bxd5 21.Bxd5 Rxd5 22.Rc8++–) 20.Rcxd5 Rxd5 21.Bxd5+ Bxd5 22.Qh5+! Kf8 23.Qxd5 Ra7 24.Qf5+ (but not 24.Qd8+? Qe8²) 24...Kg8 25.Qc8++– 19...Bxd5 20.Rcxd5+– The knight on g5 is defended.

White breaks through, as Black cannot allow the check on f7. 21...Nxe5 a) 21...dxe4 22.Qf7+ Kh8 (22...Kh6 23.Bxf5+– followed by a check on g4 or a rook lift to h3.) 23. Nxg6+ (23.Nxb6 Nxb6 24.Qxb7+–) 23...hxg6 24. Qxg6+– Black’s extra piece, which is hiding on the queenside, can’t protect the king. A direct threat is 25. Bxf5 followed by 26. Rc3. b) 21...fxe4 22.Nxd7 (or 22.Bxd7 Nxd7 23.Nxd7 Qxd7 24.Nxb6+–) 22...Nxd7 23.Bxd7 Qxd7 24.Nxb6 and 25.Nxa8+– 22.dxe5 fxe4 23.Nxb6 Ra7+– More moves are not needed, but one way to win is 24.Qe3 planning a discovered attack against the a7-rook. White chose another good move with 24.e6 (1–0, 31 moves).

title: Botvinnik – Ragozin, Moscow 1945

title: Tal – Leonov, Vilnius 1949

Qh4 both retain a huge advantage. 22...Nxf6 After 22...gxf6, White can transpose or use one of the extra options: 23.Bxh7+ and 23.Rg4+ are both winning. 23.exf6 Nxf6 23...Rc7 24.fxg7 was the game, and Black resigned on the next move. 24.Rxf6 Qg7 25.Rxh6 f5 26.Qh4+– White is a pawn up and can manoeuvre the other rook into the attack. Not 18...Bxg4? 19.Bxg3! and White holds on. 19.Bxg3 fxg3 20.hxg3 20.Nxg3 Qxh2+ 21.Kf1 Qxd2–+ 20...Qh2+ 21.Kf1 Rf6!–+ The only way to win after 17...Ng3+. solution: Bukhuti Gurgenidze – Mikhail Tal, Moscow 1957 14...Nxf2! 15.Kxf2? Ba6 and ... Nxd5, although that is not so easy to see (0–1, 27 moves).

title: Tal – T eschner, Vienna 1957
solution: Mikhail Tal – Rudolf T eschner, Vienna 1957 23.Ne4! 23.Bg7?! Rg8 24.Ne4 is worse, since the knight has to check on f6 instead of d6: 24...Qd4 25.Nf6+ Bxf6 26.exf6 Rxg7 27.fxg7 Qxg7 and Black is worse but not lost. 23...dxe4 Otherwise the knight continues to d6, opening up the e-file with devastating effect. I will give one sample line to see some attacking ideas for White: 23...Qd4 24.Nd6+ Bxd6 25.exd6 Nfe6 26.Rad1 Qa7 27.Rde1 Kd7 28.Rxe6 fxe6 29. Qf6 Winning the rook with a continuing attack. 24.Rad1+– 24.Bxf7+ is also winning, as well as many other moves. 24.Rac1 Qb6 25.Rcd1 mating, was the game finish. The Woodpecker Method 291

title: Tal – N.N., Riga (simul) 1958
solution: Mikhail Tal – N.N., Riga (simul) 1958 18.Nxf7! Kxf7 19.Qxe6+ Kf8 20.Bc1!+– Black has no defence against 21.Rf3+ Bf6 22.Ba3+ (1–0, 27 moves). 20.Rf3+? is a mistake: 20...Bf6 21.Rxf6+ Qxf6!–+ But 20.Bf4 gives White a winning advantage, as does 20.Bxe7+. But to get full points for the last one you have to see all of the following moves: 20...Rxe7 21.Rf3+ Ke8 22.Qf7+! title: Tal – Ljavdansky, Kiev 1964
solution: Mikhail Tal – Vladimir Ljavdansky, Kiev 1964 29.e7! 29.Nd5!? almost works: 29... Bxd5 30.Qxd5 Qd8! and Black defends. White can try the same idea as in the main line: 30.e7!? Bxg2+! 31.Qxg2 (31.Kxg2? Qb7+ 32.Kg1 Qxe7–+) 31...Re8 with the same type of play. However, with the open white king, Black has perpetual checks: 32.Qd5+ Kg7 33.Rxh7+ Kxh7 34.Qf7+ Kh6 35.Qxe8 Qf2!= 29...Re8 30.Nd5! The queen cannot defend f6, so Black must take. 30...Bxd5 31.Qxd5+ Kg7 32.Rxh7+! The queen needs to penetrate to f7. 32...Kxh7 33.Qf7+ Kh6 34.Qxe8 White creates luft for the king with check, and queens. 34...Qf2 35.Qh8+ Kg5 36.h4+! Kg4 37.e8=Q+– Black has only a few checks since e1 is covered by the new queen (1–0, 41 moves).

Bd7! 32...Rxc7? 33.Nxc7+– 33.Rxd7 The queen on e3 survives – the point of White’s double-rook sacrifice. 33...Rxd7 ÷ White should exchange queens to safeguard his king, with an okay position despite the knight in the corner. In the game, White instead went for the greedy 34.Qxa7? and lost (0–1, 40 moves). Solutions to Intermediate Exercises 294

title: Tal – Suetin, Tbilisi 1969
solution: Mikhail Tal – Alexey Suetin, Tbilisi 1969 20.Qxe5! dxe5 21.exf7+ Kd7 21...Kf8 22.Bh6 mate is short, and 21...Kd8 leaves White to choose his preferred route to victory, one being: 22.f8= Q+ Rxf8 23.Rxf8+ Kd7 24.Rxa8+– 22.Bf5+! A double check; Black has to give up too much material. 22...Kc6 23.Be4+ Nd5 24.Rxd5 White wins the queen with a decisive material advantage. 24.Bxd5+ Kd7 25.Bxa8++– is also good enough.

title: Tal – Korchnoi, Herceg Novi (blitz) 1970
solution: Mikhail Tal – Viktor Korchnoi, Herceg Novi (blitz) 1970 23.Qe8! White threatens 24.Rd8. 23...Raf7 23...Kg8 prepares to escape via f7, but that dream comes to an end after 24. Bd5+! Kh8 25.Bc4+– . 24.Rd8+– It is not possible to defend against both 25.Rxc8 and 25.Qxf7. Also good enough is 24.Rd5 Qb6 25.Qxf7+–, and 24.Qxf7 Rxf7 25.Rd8+ Rf8 26.Ree8 g6 27.Rxf8+ Kg7 28.Rxc8 wins as well, but is slightly unnecessary.

title: Basman – Tal, Hastings 1973
solution: Michael Basman – Mikhail Tal, Hastings 1973 28.Rxf7! Rxf7 28...Qxf7 29.Bd5! Qxd5 30.Qg7 mate ; 28...Qxe3+ 29.Kh1 Rxf7 30.Qxb8+ Be8 (30...Qe8 31.Qxe8+ Bxe8 32.Bd5 should be winning as well) 31.Bd5+– The king gets a square and the black rook is pinned. White must still take some care, but he is winning. 29.Qxb8+ Be8 29...Rf8 30.Qa7 is important, defending the e3-pawn. 30.Bd4! Defending against 30...Qxe3+ 31.Kh1 Nf2+. 30...axb2± White is close to winning if he plays accurately, but it’s difficult in practical play. Still it’s a good outcome from the diagram position. Basman played 31.Rd1, and 31.Rf1 was also a reasonable alternative.

title: Tal – Keres, Tallinn 1973
solution: Mikhail Tal – Paul Keres, Tallinn 1973 17...Nh4! The only move that saves the trapped queen. 18.gxh4 18.Bxf3? Nxf3+ 19.Kg2 Nxd2–+ wins a piece. 18...Qh3 19.Nf6+! White had to do something before Black took on h4. 19...gxf6! 19...Kh8?! 20.Nxe8± was the game (1–0, 45 moves). 20.Qxh6 exd4! Stopping 21.Re3. 21.Kh1! 21.cxd4 Nxd4 22.Re3 Nf5! 23.exf5 Rxe3µ 21...Ne5! 22.Rg1+ Bg4! 22...Ng4? 23.Bxg4 Bxg4 24.Rg3!+– 23.Rg3! a) White has a narrow way to draw with: 23.cxd4 Nf3! 24.Rg2 Rxe4 25.Bb3! Nxh4 26.Rg3 Rce8 27.Rag1! Re1 28.Bxf7+! Kxf7 29.Qh7+ Kf8 30.Qh8+ Kf7= b) 23.Bxg4?! Nxg4 24.Rxg4+ (24.Rg3?? Qxh2 mate – this is the reason why White should start with Rg3 on the 23rd move) 24...Qxg4 25.Rg1 Qxg1+³ 23...Qf1+ 24.Rg1 Qh3= Black should have seen about this far before getting his queen trapped on f3, but from the diagram position, Black has no choice but to go for 17... Nh4 and make it up along the way. So you don’t need to see anything of this to get full points.

title: Tal – Stean, Moscow 1975
solution: Mikhail Tal – Michael Stean, Moscow 1975 18.Nxh6+! gxh6 19.Qg6+ Kh8 19...Bg7 20.Bxf7+ Kf8 21.Bxh6! (21.Bf4 seems almost as strong and simpler: 21...Re7 22.Bd6±) 21...Bxh6 22.Bd5! Qe7 23.Qxh6+ Qg7± With Black’s king in mind, White should keep the queens on. 20.Bxf7+– There is no defence against 21.Bxh6. If 20...Rh5 then White wins by challenging the knight on f6 in some fashion. In the game, Black tried 20...Rc6 and was immediately rewarded: 21.Rd5? Rxe3! (which he didn’t play) 22.fxe3 Bg7!÷ Instead, 21.Bf4!, 21.Bxh6 and 21.Nd5 are all winning.

But the game move is good enough. 36...Kg7 36...Rxc6 37.d7+– queens. After having moved the king, Black threatens 37...Rxc6 38.d7 Rfd6 39.cxd6 Rxd6 with drawing chances. 37.Re7+! The game continued: 37.d7 Rfxc6! 38.dxc8=Q Rxc8 39.b4 The rook ending should be winning, but it is not over yet (1–0, 50 moves). Instead, checking on e7 is accurate when Black’s king cannot go to f6. title: Spassky – Korchnoi, Moscow 1964
solution: Boris Spassky – Viktor Korchnoi, Moscow 1964 14.Nxd5! White threatens 15.Nc7 and 15.Nxf6+ Qxf6 16.Bxb7. 14...Bxd5 14...Bd8 15.Nf6+ wins an exchange, but 15.Nc7 shows even less mercy; Black loses a piece. 15.Nf4! Rc1+ 27.Qf1 Rxf1+ 28.Kxf1 Bxg7 29.Rg3 should also win in the end, but can be messed up by White for sure (so not full points). title: Spassky – Zuk, Vancouver 1971
solution: Boris Spassky – Robert Zuk, Vancouver 1971 40.Ng5! Bc8 The only defence against 41.Rh3+. 40...Rh6 41.Nf7++– and 40...Rxg5 41.Qh4+ (or 41.Rh3++–) are hopeless. However, also after the game move White has a generally winning position. Strongest is 41.Qe4+– threatening 42.Ne6 as a decisive discovered attack. Black will have to give up material to survive. 41.a5 is also definitely winning, but not the game move 41.Nf7+?! as it allows 41...Kg8! (which was not played) 42.Nxe5+ Be6± and Black has fighting chances only a pawn down. Solutions to Intermediate Exercises 306

title: Spassky – Fischer, Reykjavik (1) 1972
solution: Boris Spassky – Robert Fischer, Reykjavik (1) 1972 I expect that you recognized the first move, but it would have been a mistake were it not for a critical move later in the variation. 32.Kf3! Putting Black under pressure. Instead 32.gxh4 should be a draw. 32...Ke7 The critical position arises after 32...h3 33.Kg4 Bg1 34.Kxh3 Bxf2 when Fischer may have missed that the bishop is trapped after: 35.Bd2!+– Zero points if you didn’t see this move! (Harsh – but on the other hand 32.gxh4 is worth one point.) 33.Kg2 hxg3 34.fxg3 Bxg3 35.Kxg3 Kd6 36.a4 Kd5 37.Ba3 Ke4?! Fischer lost this famous game. 37...a6! has been analysed to a draw.

title: Spassky – Borik, Germany 1982
solution: Boris Spassky – Otto Borik, Germany 1982 28.Nxf7! Spassky played 28.Qxf7+ Qxf7 29.Nxf7 when 29...Nxc3!² would have limited the material loss to a pawn. 28...Qxf7 29.Rd1± Exchanging on f7 would have helped the black king to e6, and forced c3-c4 to win back the piece. And that would have left the b4-pawn en prise. The opposite-coloured bishops give Black drawing chances, but fortunately White can keep the rooks on in order to make better use of his advantage.

solution: Robert Fischer – Boris Spassky, Belgrade (19) 1992 30.Rxe5! 30.Bxe5?! dxe5 31.Rxe5² is too soft – Black has more counterplay with the rooks on the board and it’s easier to control a passed d-pawn than an a-pawn. 30...dxe5 31.Bxe5 Qe7 31...Qxe5 32.Qxa7++– and the rook on b6 is lost. 32.d6! Black’s queen has no squares to defend the a7-pawn, and after the only move 32...Rxd6 White will emerge with an extra passed pawn: 33.Bxd6 Qxd6 34.Qxa7+±

title: Ioseliani – Spassky, Copenhagen 1997
solution: Nana Ioseliani – Boris Spassky, Copenhagen 1997 Black would have had compensation for the exchange if he was allowed to pick up the d-pawn for free. 37.d7! Counterattacking with 37.Ra1 is an interesting option. With the knight on h5, Black should probably seek safety for his king in the centre with 37...Kf8!±. 37...Qd6 37...Nxd7 38.Qe8+ and Black loses the f-pawn, while 37... Qxd7 38.Nf6+ forks the queen. 38.Rxc4 Many other moves were also winning. Black loses one of his pieces due to the pin on the d-file after: 38...Nxd7 38...Nxc4 39.Qe8++– and White queens. 39.Qd1 1–0

title: Spassky – Korchnoi, St Petersburg (5) 1999
solution: Boris Spassky – Viktor Korchnoi, St Petersburg (5) 1999 25...Nxf2! 26.Rf1 26.Nxf2 Qe2! (26...Rxf2+?! 27.Kxf2 Qd4+ 28.Kg2 Qxa1 29.Ne4 and White has compensation, with firm control over the light squares.) 27. Rf1 Bh6–+ Black wins back the piece with an extra pawn and an attack. 26...Qh3+ 26...Nxe4 is also a reasonable advantage for Black. 27.Kg1 Ng4! White’s knights are stepping on each other, and Black uses his solo knight for offensive purposes. Black has a clear advantage, but Spassky managed to draw.

title: Spassky – Eliet, France 2002
solution: Boris Spassky – Nicolas Eliet, France 2002 18.f4+! The only winning move. 18. Be7 traps the king, but there is no mate after 18... Ne8±. 18...Kxf4 19.Bc7+ Spassky’s 19.Rf1+ induced resignation, as 19...Ke5 20.Bc7+ Ke6 21.Bc4+ Ke7 22.Rxf7+ Ke8 23.Bd6 creates the decisive threat of 24.Re7+ followed by 25.Bxg8 (you need to see this far if you chose 19.Rf1). 19...Kg5 19...Ke3 20.Bg3 with mate on d3. 20.Rg1+ Kf6 21.e5+ Or White can start with 21. Bd6+– although that gives Black some better options than transposing with 21...Ke6. 21...Ke7 22.Bd6+ Kd8 23.Ne4 The knight on g7 drops after 24.Nf6. And it’s equally good to win the knight with 23.Bd3+–. Solutions to Intermediate Exercises 310

title: Spassky – Coleman, Reno (simul) 2004
solution: Boris Spassky – Scott Coleman, Reno (simul) 2004 15.Nxd5! A second and more complicated solution is: 15.exf6 Rxf6 (15...gxf6 16. Nxe6+ Kf7 17.Qh5+ Kxe6 18.Qxd5 mate) 16.Qh4 (or 16.Qh3) 16...Rf5 17.Qh7+ You need to see this far. 17...Kf6 18.g4 Rxg5 19.fxg5+ Ke5 Black is one move from escaping, but does not get enough time: 20.Qg6! Ba6 (defending against Nb5) 21.Rf7 Qe8 22.Rd1!+– White has a crushing attack; ...Kd6 is not possible right now, and all White’s pieces are homing in on the black king. 15...exd5 16.f5+ Bxf5 17.Qxf5+ Kh5 18.Qh7+ 18.Rf3 is also quite strong, with mate in one, and there are other ways. 18...Kg4 19.h3+ Kxg5 20.Rf5 mate At the start, 15.Nxe6+ is a good try but doesn’t seem to win straight away. 15...Kf7 Preventing White from capturing on f8 with check. 16.exf6 Qxe6 (16...Qxf6 17.f5+–) 17.Qxg7+ Ke8 18.Rfe1 Ne4 19.Nxd5! White sacrifices a third piece! 19...Qxd5 20.Rad1 Qf5 21.Rd4! The rook is immune and White wins back at least a piece and a rook. One line given by the engine is: 21...Rxf6 22.Rdxe4+ Be6 23.Qg8+ Rf8 24.Qxe6+ Qxe6 25.Rxe6+ Kd7 26.g3±

title: Spassky – Christensen, Reno (simul) 2004
solution: Boris Spassky – Craig Christensen, Reno (simul) 2004 27.Rxf7! Nxc3 27...Kxf7 28.Qe6+ (28.Bxd5+ also wins) 28...Kg7 29.Bxd5 Threatening mate on f7. After 29...Rf8, White is winning after any move that defends the pawn on f2. One efficient way is 30.Be3 followed by 31.Bd4+. 27...e6!? 28.Rxc7 Nxc7 and at least one of Black’s weak centre pawns will lost, for instance: 29.Bf4 d5 30.Bxc7 Qxc7 31.Bxd5+– 28.Qe6 1–0 Mate is coming.

title: Kramer – Fischer, New York 1957
solution: George Kramer – Robert Fischer, New York 1957 19...Nxc3! T otally destroying the seemingly strong dark-square fortification. 20.Qxc3 Nxd4–+ White has three loose pieces: a1-rook, queen on c3, and c5-bishop. 21.Qb4 Ne2+ Stronger is 21...a5! 22.Qa3 Nb5–+ and Black picks up the rook without having to sacrifice on c5. 22.Kh1 Rxc5 23.Qxc5 Bxa1 Black is probably still winning, and that was the result nine moves later. The Woodpecker Method Robert Fischer All that matters on the chessboard is good moves. 311

title: Fischer – Sherwin, New York 1957
solution: Robert Fischer – James Sherwin, New York 1957 30.Rxf7!? The best move. Although it does not lead to a decisive advantage against correct defence, it is best both objectively and practically, as Black can easily go wrong. After 30.Bxf7+?! Kh8³, Black might take over. 30...Rc1+? Natural but losing. Black had to find: 30...h5! 31.Rc4 (31.Rf5+?? Kh7–+ and White is back-rank mated if he takes the queen) 31...Rxc4 32.Rxf8+ Kxf8 33.Qxc4² 31.Qf1!! Everything checks out for White. But not 31.Rf1+? Kh8–+. 31...h5 Three alternatives: a) 31...Rxf1+ 32.Rxf1+ Qxd5 33.Rxf8+ Kxf8 34.exd5+–; b) 31...Rxf7 32.Ra8+ mating; c) 31...Nf2+ 32.Rxf2++– 32.Qxc1! Qxc1+ 33.Rf1+ Kh7 34.Rxc1+–

solution: Robert Fischer – Arthur Bisguier, New York 1963 29.e6! A full-blown attack with only a few pieces and a couple of pawns! title: Fischer – Benko, New York 1963
solution: Robert Fischer – Pal Benko, New York 1963 19.Rf6! Blocking the defensive move ...f7-f5 by drastic means. 19.e5 allows 19...f5!÷. 19...Kg8 19...h6 20.e5 transposes and there are also other winning moves, while 19...Bxf6 20.e5 Qxe5 21.Qxh7 mate is obviously over. 20.e5! h6 21.Ne2 With a winning attack. 21. Ne4+– or anything else reasonable also wins; Black is quite helpless against White’s attack.

title: Fischer – Naranja, Manila 1967
solution: Robert Fischer – Renato Naranja, Manila 1967 This exercise is about making a decision, and avoiding a tempting sacrifice. 14.Bg5! Bringing the bishop into the attack in the most effective way. T wo alternatives: a) 14.g4 looks winning and is winning, even though Black gets some counterplay with 14...d5. White chooses between 15.Ba2 dxe4 16.dxe4 Qd4 17.g5 Bxe4 18.Ne2!+– and 15.g5 g6 16.fxg6 fxg6 17.Qg4+– (full points for both choices on move 15). b) 14.Bxh6?! gxh6 15.Qxh6 Bg7 16.Qg5 Nc6! The only way to defend against 17.f6, but now White’s best is to exchange queens. That’s disappointing, even though White still has a strong attack after 17.Nd5! Qxg5 18.hxg5±. 14...d5 14...hxg5? 15.hxg5 with mate next move. 14...Nc6 defends the bishop but Black’s pawn structure will nevertheless suffer after: 15.Bxf6 Qxf6 16.Nd5 Qd8 17.f6+– 15.Bxf6 dxc4 15...gxf6 16.Qxh6 dxc4 17.Rh3+– 16.Qg4+– White is totally dominating and will win enough material (1–0, 32 moves). The Woodpecker Method 313

title: Fischer – Panno, Buenos Aires 1970
solution: Robert Fischer – Oscar Panno, Buenos Aires 1970 29.Nxh7! 29.Nf5! might be even prettier and full points if you saw the following lines: 29...exf5 30.gxf5 gxf5 (30...f6 31.Bxd5++–) 31.Bxf5 f6 32.Be6+! Blocking the e-file. (Not 32.exf6 Qe1+ 33.Kg2 Qf1+! with a perpetual.) 32...Nxe6 33.exf6 Qd7 34.Nxe6+– (or 34.f7++–) But 29.Bxd5? exd5 30.Nf5 gxf5 31.gxf5 which does not work, as 31...Nd6 32.f6 Nf5 defends and wins. 29...Nxh7 30.hxg6 fxg6 30...dxe4 31.Qxh7+ Kf8 32.Qh8 mate 31.Bxg6 Now Nh5-f6 or Bxh7 followed by Qxe6+ are on the agenda. 31...Ng5 31...Qg7 32.Bxh7+ Qxh7 33.Qxe6++– and the knight on c8 is en prise, as it also is after 31...Be8 32.Bxh7+ Qxh7 33.Qxe6++– . 32.Nh5! White has enough attacking pieces to finish Black off, but first some checks must be parried. 32.Kg2+– is another way to do that. 32...Nf3+ 33.Kg2!+– 33.Kh1? Qh4+–+ 33...Nh4+ 34.Kg3 Nxg6 35.Nf6+ Kf7 36.Qh7+ 1–0 The end was not far away: 36...Kf8 37.Qg8 mate

title: Fischer – Taimanov, Vancouver (2) 1971
solution: Robert Fischer – Mark Taimanov, Vancouver (2) 1971 82.Bc8! 82.Bf5+ Kf4 83.h4 Ng4+! is a draw, since the king must keep the bishop protected. 82.Be6 Nf3 and the pawn can’t advance. 82...Kf4 83.h4 Nf3 83...Ng4+ 84.Kg7 and the pawn will soon advance. 84.h5 Ng5 85.Bf5 It is also possible to start with 85.h6. 85...Nf3 86.h6 Ng5 87.Kg6 Zugzwang; the pawn promotes. 87...Nf3 88.h7 Ne5+ 89.Kf6 1–0

title: Korchnoi – Karpov, Moscow (21) 1974
solution: Viktor Korchnoi – Anatoly Karpov, Moscow (21) 1974 13.Nxh7! Re8 13...Kxh7 14.Qh6+ Kg8 15.Qxg6+ Kh8 16.Qh5+ (16.Qh6+ mates in a slower way, but White should avoid 16. Bxf7? Bxd7 28.Nd8+! 1–0 White wins material and gives mate.

title: Karpov – Geller, Moscow 1981
solution: Anatoly Karpov – Efim Geller, Moscow 1981 31.Rxf7!+– Queen and knight is the usual combo, but here a queen with a bishop wreaks havoc when the king’s defending pawns are gone. The fact that the knight on d5 only protects dark squares plays a large part in giving such a free rein to the bishop. Good enough only for a clear advantage are 31.Qa4 and 31.Qc4. 31...Kxf7 32.Qxg6+ Kf8 32...Ke7 33.Qg7+ Ke8 34.Bg6 mate 33.Qxh6+ 1–0 Black resigned due to 33...Ke8 34.Bb5++– and 33...Kg8 34.Bh7+ Kf7 35.Bg6+ Kg8 36.Qh7+ Kf8 37.Qf7 mate.

title: Karpov – Chandler, Bath 1983

Nxg3? 29.hxg3 Qxg3 30.Rxf5+– (1–0, 36 moves). 29.Kxh2 Nxg3 29...Bxg3+? 30.Kg1+– 30.Qb5 There is no rescue after 30. title: Karpov – Hansen, Thessaloniki (ol) 1988
solution: Anatoly Karpov – Lars Bo Hansen, Thessaloniki (ol) 1988 20.Nxf7! Picking up a pawn. 20.g4 is also quite strong and if you evaluated 20... Qe7 21.Nxf7 as winning, you get full points. 20...Qd4 20...Kxf7 21.Rc7+ Kf8 22.Rxb7+– The check on d1 is not dangerous. 21.Qd6! Clearly best, but not necessary to see before taking on f7. title: Short – Kasparov, Belfort 1988

Without the second pair of rooks, White will not have enough compensation for the exchange. 25.b3 Giving up the b2- pawn with, for instance, 25.R1d3 might be a better idea, but Black is much better. And he wins after 25.Rxb4? Bxe3+ 26.Kb1 Rxb4. 25...e5! Overloading the queen. 26.Qxe5 Qxc3–+

title: Shirov – Kasparov, Manila (ol) 1992
solution: Alexei Shirov – Garry Kasparov, Manila (ol) 1992 35...Bd4!! The white queen is in the crosshairs of the black queen and bishop. The rook cannot be taken due to the further pin by the bishop, and the knight cannot take the bishop since the queen would drop. And finally a queen trade would allow the intermediate ... Bxf2+ winning a rook. Instead the game continued 35... Qxe3 36.Nxe3 Bd4 37.Rxd2 Bxe3+ 38.Kh2 Bxd2 39.gxf3 Rg3!µ and Black managed to convert his advantage, although things are far from over. 36.Qxg5 Other moves also lose immediately: 36. title: Kasparov – Kramnik, Moscow (blitz 1) 1998
solution: Garry Kasparov – Vladimir Kramnik, Moscow (blitz 1) 1998 39.d5! Kasparov played 39.Rxf5+ Bxf5 40.Nf7+ Kf4 41.Nxd8= and Black held a draw after 41...Ke4 42.Nxc6 Ne6. A critical, but not forced, variation is 43. Nc8 Nxd4 44.Nd6+ Kd5 45.Nxd4 Kxd4 46.Nxf5+ Kxc5 when White can’t keep the last pawn. 39...cxd5 40.Nb7 Re8 41.c6 The c-pawn and the pin on the e-file win a piece, and thus the game. For example, 41...Kf6 42.Re1 Re7 43.Nc5 followed by Nxe6 and Nxd5.

title: Kasparov – Kramnik, Moscow (blitz 19) 1998
solution: Vladimir Kramnik – Garry Kasparov, Moscow (blitz 19) 1998 38.f5! The only way to keep material on the board. 38...Bxe5 39.Qb7! Keeping the g-pawn. 39.Qxa7?! exf5 and Black will be able to reach an ending with rook and f-pawn versus queen. 39...Rd6 40.fxe6 Rxe6 41.Qxa7 Black has to give up the bishop for the a-pawn. With the help of zugzwang, White is probably able to win the g-pawn. But it doesn’t matter – it’s a fortress anyway. If Black’s king stays on g7, White can never sacrifice the queen to get a winning pawn ending. The same ending is reached after: 38...Rxe5 39. Qe7! (39.Qd8? is a double threat against d4 and g5, but 39...Re3+ 40.Kg2 Bf6= defends) 39...Re3+ 40.Kg2 Bf6 41.Qxa7 Re4 42.fxe6 Rxe6 So 38.f5 is only a draw, but it’s a good try that was rewarded in this blitz game: 38...exf5 39.e6 1–0 The exercise is about decision-making. Calculating all the variations above is not necessary before playing the first move.

title: Khalifman – Larsen, London 1991
solution: Alexander Khalifman – Bent Larsen, London 1991 29.Ne7+! Starting a merry hunt for loose black pieces. 29...Kf7 29...Kh5 avoids the capture on d7 coming with check, but the king is too exposed; White wins with 30.Ne4 or 30.h3. 30.Nc6! Forcing away the defender is better than 30.Ne4±. 30...Rc8 31.Rxd7+ Ke8 A counter-trick! 32.Nxe5! Moving one threatened piece to defend the other by overloading the bishop. 32. Rc7? Nxc7 33.dxc7 Rxc7 is not better for White, but 32. Rxh7?! Rxc6± has won a pawn compared to the starting position. 32...Bxe5 33.Re7+ Kd8 After 33...Kf8 White has a number of ways to win, for instance: 34.Bh6+ Kg8 35.Rxe6 Bxc3 36.d7+– 34.Bb6+ 1–0 Black loses several pieces.

title: Popov – Khalifman, Aix les Bains 2011
solution: Valerij Popov – Alexander Khalifman, Aix les Bains 2011 19...Neg4+! 19...Nfg4+ 20.Kg1 Nxe3 21.fxe3µ is less convincing, as here the knight would be better on f6 because of the control over e4 and pressure on e3. 20.hxg4 20.Kg1 Nxe3 21.fxe3 The e3-pawn can be taken at will, so Black is much better. 20...Nxg4+ 21.Kg1 Bxg2 22.Kxg2 Rxe3!µ The rook cannot be taken, so Black has won a pawn for no compensation. White collapsed quickly: 23.Nf4 Rd8 24.Rh1 Re4 25.Rc1 Nxf2 0–1 Another tactic against the white king and queen finished the game. 26. Kxf2 is met by 26... Rxd4 27.Qxd4 Bb6 winning the queen. solution: Vladimir Kramnik – Ljubomir Ljubojevic, Monaco (rapid) 2000 30.Bxf6 Bxf6 31.Re7+! Still going for the dark squares. 32...Bh4 33.Qd4! Rg8 34.Qa7 Strongest, but by now other moves also win. 34...Rh8 35.Ree7 White is mating. 35...g5 36.Rf6+ Bg6 37.Rxg6+ Kxg6 38.Re6+ Kf5 39.Qf7 mate

title: Leko – Kramnik, Budapest (4) 2001
solution: Peter Leko – Vladimir Kramnik, Budapest (4) 2001 22...Bb4! Bad are 22...gxf6 23.Rde2± and 22...Bxd5 23.Rxd5+–. 23.f7 23.Nxb4 Rxd2 24.Nxd2 Rxe1+–+ 23...Rxe4! 23...Bxd2 24.fxe8=Q Rxe8 25.Re2± 24.Rxe4 Bxd2 25.Re7! A nice last trick, but it doesn’t save the position. 25...Bxd5 26.Re8 Bxf7 27.Rxd8µ The bishop pair is usually much stronger than a rook and pawn. title: Gelfand – Kramnik, Moscow 2008
solution: Boris Gelfand – Vladimir Kramnik, Moscow 2008 32...Nce3? A tempting but bad try that Kramnik fell for. 32...Qf8µ is best, but anything other than the main line that does not seem bad gives full points. T wo more alternatives are 32...Bxf2+ 33.Qxf2 Rxc6 34.Bxc6 Qxc6³ and 32... Nfd6³. 33.fxe3 Nxe3 34.Bd4! 34.Rd2 Nd5+ 35.Kh1 Qxc6 with a winning position, was Black’s idea. 34...Bxd4 35.Rxd4 35.Nxd4? Nxd1 36.Qxd1 is winning for Black due to the two pawns and White’s unstable knight. Nxg2 36.Nb4!= The knight on g2 is trapped, so Black will have to show some care to draw this with some pawns for a knight.

title: Kramnik – Svidler, Moscow (blitz) 2008
solution: Vladimir Kramnik – Peter Svidler, Moscow (blitz) 2008 24...Nf2! Black’s tactical threat is 25...dxe4, but the knight might also just continue to d3. Not 24...dxe4? 25.Qxc4+±. 25.Be3!? A smart try, but not good enough. 25...Nd3! Black threatens the rook but also 25...Ba6 followed by 26...dxe4. White’s knight can’t move due to a discovered attack. solution: Loek van Wely – Viswanathan Anand, Monte Carlo (rapid) 1999 22...d3! 22...Ne8 23.Rc8 d3 transposes to 23...Ne8 in the main line. 23.Rc8+ 23.Rd2 Rbb1–+ 23...Kf7! Full points also for 23...Ne8 24.Rxb8 dxc2 25.Rxe8+ Kf7 26.Rc8 Rxc1+ 27.Kf2 when White’s king is close enough to stop the c-pawn, but Black gets a winning pawn or rook ending after 27...a5 28.Ke3 Re1+! 29.Kd2 Rg1. But 23...Rxc8? 24.Rxc8+ Kf7 25.Kf2 is only equal. 24.R2c7+ Kg6 25.Kf2 25.Rxb8 d2–+ 25...Rxc1! 0–1 After 26. Rxc1 d2!–+ Black wins a rook, remaining a piece up.

The immediate double threat 22...Qe5 loses to 23.Qd8+. 23.gxh3 Qe5 Apparently a double attack. 24.c3!+– But it could be parried! White is winning, and did indeed win in 33 moves. 24.Bf3? is not good enough: 24...Rh4–+

title: Ponomariov – Dominguez Perez, Tashkent 2012
solution: Ruslan Ponomariov – Leinier Dominguez Perez, Tashkent 2012 33.Rxe7! Eliminating the defence of the dark squares. 33. Bc7?! Rxc7 34.Qxc7 Qxc7 35.Rxc7 Nc8 wins an exchange, but White is only slightly better. 33...Qxe7 33...Rxe7 34.Nf6+ and as there are many ways to conclude the attack, it’s enough to see this far. A few lines: 34... Kh8 (34...Kg7 35.Qg5+– and the queen is coming to h6 with devastating effect) 35.Qh4 h5 36.Qg5 Qf8 37.Bd6 The defence is collapsing, since both e7 and f5 are hanging. It’s over after 37...Rcc7 38.Rxf5+–. 34.Bg5! 34.Be5!? or 34.d6!? and some other moves are good but not best or most natural. 34...Qe2 35.Nf6+ Kg7 36.Nxe8+ Rxe8 37.Rxf5 1–0 Black has to give up the queen to delay mate after 37...gxf5 38.Be7+! . A few lines: 34... Kh8 (34...Kg7 35.Qg5+– and the queen is coming to h6 with devastating effect) 35.Qh4 h5 36.Qg5 Qf8 37.Bd6 The defence is collapsing, since both e7 and f5 are hanging. title: Kasimdzhanov – Bakhtadze, Yerevan 1999
solution: Rustam Kasimdzhanov – Giorgi Bakhtadze, Yerevan 1999 40.Ne6+! A discovered attack with an added threat to the f4-knight. Black has a fork, but White emerges with a winning position. 40...Ke7 40...Nxe6 41.Rxd7 Nf6 (41...Rxc4 42.Nxc4 Nf6 43.Ne5+– or 43.Ra7 Nxg4+ 44.Kg3!+–) 42.Bxe6! (42.Rf4+– is also good enough) 42...fxe6 43.Rf4!+– 41.Rxd7+ Kxd7 42.Nxf4 1–0 Solutions to Intermediate Exercises Rustam Kasimdzhanov (on Anand) He sees a lot more than all the others, but that isn’t necessarily a strength. In the games he loses he has also seen more than his opponent. Playing chess isn’t about what you see. Playing chess is about what you can seize from that. It can also sometimes be a burden when you see so many variations that you can no longer maintain control. Chess24 (2013) 336

solution: Veselin T opalov – Jacob Bjerre Jensen, Copenhagen 1991 28...Nf4!! What a multipurpose move! Black cuts off the queen from the mate threat, threatens the bishop, opens the h-file for either the queen on h6 or a rook on h5. White is utterly defenceless against so many threats. title: Nedobora – T opalov, Candas 1992
solution: Mikhail Nedobora – Veselin T opalov, Candas 1992 25...e4! Nxf3 29.Rxf6 (29.Rg3 Bg7µ) 29...Nxg1 30.Nxg1 is unclear. 28...Kf8 28...Bxg5 29.Qxg5+ is a key move, after which White’s attack is winning in many ways; an evaluation that can be made without calculating further. But here we can afford some supporting variations. (29.Rh8+? Kg7 30.Rh7+ [30.Qh7+? Kf6–+ and the attack is over] 30...Kf6 31.Rxf7+! Nxf7 32.Qxf3 Ne5 And White is better, but not winning.) 29... Ng6 (29...Kf8 30.Rh8 mate) 30.Bxg6 fxg6 (30...Qd3+ 31.Ka1 Qd1+ 32.Nc1 changes nothing) 31.Rxg6+ Kf7 32.Rg7+ Kf8 33.Rg8+ Kf7 34.Qg7 mate 29.Rxf6+– White has won a piece, so trading queens is not really in Black’s interest, but if he does not, then the attack is winning. The only thing that might be useful to see is that Black runs out of checks after: 29...Qd3+ 30.Kc1 Qe3+ 31.Kd1 Qd3+ 32.Ke1 Qb1+ 33.Kf2+–

The threat is to sacrifice the knight and take on f7. 31.Bg4, and others, still leave White much better, but secure no points. 31...Be8 31...fxe6 32.Nxe6+ with mate. 32.Nd5 32.Rh3+– and other moves are also winning. Black has lost connection between his rooks. 32. Bb3 is also a good move, with the threat of checking on e6. 32...Nxd5 33.Bxd5 1–0 Rf3-h3 followed by Qf2-f6+ is one decisive idea.

title: Steinitz – Meitner, Vienna 1859
solution: Wilhelm Steinitz – Philipp Meitner, Vienna 1859 20.e6! dxe6 20...fxe6 21.Qxh5++– and White picks up the knight on a5. 20...Nxc4 and White wins with three moves, of which you should have seen one: a) 21. Nf5 and if the queen moves, White takes on f7/d7 and e7. And 21...Nxf5 22.exd7++– is a double check. b) 21.exd7+ Bxd7 22.Qxb7+– is complicated. c) Easiest is 21.exf7+ Qxf7 22.Nf5+– when Black can’t defend e7. 21.Bb5+ The move order 21. Qd3 Nac6 22.Bxc7 transposes. Full points also for 21. Bxc7 Nac6 22.Qd3 f6 when White has a winning position due to the black king, even though it’s not over yet. 21...c6 21...Nac6 22.Nf5!+– and as the e7-knight is overloaded, White will soon win the knight on c6 (or the rook on a8). 22.Bc7 Another winning line is 22.Bd6 cxb5 23.Bxe7 Kxe7 24.Nf5+ taking the queen. 22...Bd7 23.Bxa5 Qg4! Material is equal after 23...cxb5, but White wins with the double threat 24.Qxb7 (or 24.Rxd7 Kxd7 25.Qxb7+). 24.Qd3! The only winning move; Black doesn’t get time to take on h4 for free. 24...Nd5 25.Re4!+– White is a piece up.

title: Zukertort – Steinitz, London (1) 1872
solution: Johannes Zukertort – Wilhelm Steinitz, London (1) 1872 20...Bxf2+! 21.Kh1 21.Kxf2 fxe5+ comes with check, followed by: 22.Kg1 Qxg5–+ 21...Be8! Winning a second pawn. Steinitz played: 21... Bxe1?! 22.Nxf7 Kxf7 23.Qd5+ (White can keep the queens on after 23. Rxe1?! Bc6 24.Qe6+ Kg6 25.Be3µ, but it would have been a dubious decision. With an extra pawn defending his king, it’s Black who may look forward to an attack on the enemy king.) 23...Kg6 24.Rxe1 Bc6 (It is not possible to hang on to the bishop after 24...fxg5 25.Rd1.) 25.Qxd8 Rxd8 26.Be3µ White has decent drawing chances, but the same can be said about Black’s winning chances (0–1, 54 moves). 21...Bc6 22.Nxf7 Qxd6 23.Nxd6 Bxe1 24.Rxe1 fxg5µ is also a pawn up, and also not full points. 22.Nxf7 Bxf7 23.Qxd8+ Rxd8µ Because of the back-rank weakness, White has to move the bishop, after which Black takes on e1 and a2.

title: Steinitz – Von Bardeleben, Hastings 1895
solution: Wilhelm Steinitz – Curt von Bardeleben, Hastings 1895 20.Qg4! Threatening the pawn on g7, but also a discovered attack. 20...g6 21.Ng5+! Ke8 21...fxg5 22.Qxd7+– 22.Rxe7+! Kf8! Black tries to use the twin threats of mate on c1 and ...Qxg4 to get out of his troubles. 22...Qxe7 23.Rxc8++– wins a piece and 22...Kxe7 23.Qb4+ (or 23.Re1+ first) 23... Ke8 24.Re1+ Kd8 25.Ne6++– wins the queen. 23.Rf7+! 23.Qxd7?? Rxc1+ and it’s White that gets mated. 23...Kg8! 24.Rg7+! Kh8! 24...Kf8 25.Nxh7++– and the queen is captured with check. 25.Rxh7+! Von Bardeleben left the board and didn’t come back. He is lost after: 25...Kg8 26.Rg7+! Kh8 27.Qh4+! Kxg7 28.Qh7+ Kf8 29.Qh8+! Ke7 30.Qg7+ 30.Re1+ is also winning. 30...Ke8 31.Qg8+ Ke7 32.Qf7+ Kd8 33.Qf8+! Qe8 34.Nf7+ Kd7 35.Qd6 mate

title: Steinitz – Lasker, Moscow (3) 1896
solution: Wilhelm Steinitz – Emanuel Lasker, Moscow (3) 1896 34...Rg8! Black has no threats, but White is in a decisive zugzwang! His pieces are all busy protecting the g2-, g5- and h1-squares. 35.Re1 Qxf5 36.Re5 Qf3 37.d5 Qg3+ 38.Kh1 Qxe5 39.dxc6+ Kxc6 0–1 Wilhelm Steinitz A sacrifice is best refuted by accepting it. 347Solutions to Advanced Exercises

title: Lipke – Steinitz, Vienna 1898
solution: Paul Lipke – Wilhelm Steinitz, Vienna 1898 17.Nxc7! Rxc7 17...Qxc7 18.Bxd6++– wins the queen. 18.Bxd6+! Re7 With rook and two pawns for two pieces, White may be better due to the exposed black king, but there is a way to make use of that straight away to gain a winning advantage. 19.e5! The only move that is clearly winning. However, in a game you don’t need to see that before taking on c7, since it was the best move anyway. Lipke played 19.Ba3?! Qe8 20.e5, but now there was 20...fxe5! 21.Ng5 Bh6± without mate on f7; Steinitz won the game in the end. 19...fxe5 19...Qe8 defends the f7-square in advance, and prepares to offer the exchange of queens one day. 20. Bxe7+! Qxe7 (20...Nxe7 and White wins after various moves, for instance 21. Rd6!) 21.exf6! Qxf6 22.h4! h6 (22... Bh6 23.Qc5+ Kg7 24.Re8 with a winning attack) Including the moves with the h-pawns avoids ...Bh6 and ...Kg7. There are many ways to continue, among them 23.Qc5+ Kg8 24.Re8+ Kh7 25.Qc4 Bf8 26.h5+–. 20.Ng5 Bh6 20...Qe8 21.Nxh7 mate 21.Qf7! mate

title: Lasker – Bauer, Amsterdam 1889
solution: Emanuel Lasker – Johann Bauer, Amsterdam 1889 15.Bxh7+! Kxh7 16.Qxh5+ Kg8 17.Bxg7! The classic double-bishop sacrifice! 17...Kxg7 17...f6 is easy to handle: 18. Bh6 with mate or 18. Rf3. But 17...f5!? is trickier. White has three options: a) 18.Bh6? does not work. White needs the check on g4 after 18... Qe8–+; b) 18.Be5! Rf6 19.Rf3! The only move that wins, but now it will soon be mate. c) 18. Rf3 also wins, but only if White finds all the following moves: 18...Kxg7 19.Rg3+ Bg5 20.Rxg5+! Kf6 21.Qh4! Kf7 22.Qh7+! Ke8 23.Rg7! Rb8 24.Rc7! Qd6 25.Rxb7+– 18.Qg4+! Kh7 19.Rf3 e5 20. Rh3+ Qh6 21.Rxh6+ Kxh6 Black has enough pieces, but a double threat settles matters: 22.Qd7!+–

title: Lasker – Blackburne, London 1892
solution: Emanuel Lasker – Joseph Blackburne, London 1892 28.Re7! Ne6 28...Qxe7 29.Qxd5++– wins the other rook as well. 29.Re1 If the knight moves, there follows 30.Re8. 29.f5+–, pushing the f-pawn immediately, is even stronger. 29...Qxe7 30.Qxd5 Re8 31.f5+– (1–0, 39 moves)

title: Lasker – Hasselblatt, Riga (simul) 1909
solution: Emanuel Lasker – Hasselblatt, Riga (simul) 1909 Lasker played 27.Bxh7+? with the idea 27...Kxh7 28.h6++–. But after 27...Kf8! he only had one way to avoid being mated after ... Bc1/a1 or ...Rb5-a5. 28.Qh4! (after 28.Ne1 Lasker’s opponent missed the mate starting with 28... Rb5) 28...Ke8! 29.Bg6! Bc1 30.Bxf7+ Kd7 31.Bxe6+! Ke8 (31...Kc7? 32.Rxg7+ Kb6 33.Qd8++–) 32.Bf7+!= It’s a draw, even though not necessarily an immediate repetition. 27.Bg6! The correct move, but be aware of long lines. 27...Re7 a) 27...hxg6 28.hxg6 with mate. b) 27...Rbb7 28.Bxf7+ Rxf7 29.Rhg2 is also a winning attack: 29... Kh8 30.Qxg7+ Rxg7 31.Rxg7 Qf8 32.h6+– and 33. Ng5. c) 27... Ba1 (or 27... Bc1) 28.Bxf7+ Kxf7 29.Qxg7+ gives White a winning attack. 28.h6! 28.Bxh7+? Kf8 29.h6! This is a possibility now, as Black’s rook takes the e7-square for the queen. 29...g5! 30. Qxg5 Ke8 and White has only a draw. 28...Bc1 29.Bxh7+! Kf8 30.hxg7+ Ke8 31.g8=Q+ Kd7 32.Q4xe6+! Rxe6 33.Rg7+ Kc6 34.Nd4+! Kc5 35.Nxe6+! Bxe6 36.Rc7+! Kd4 37.Qg1+! Until this point, it was only only-moves from White! 37...Be3 38.Rd2+ Or 38.Qd1+ Bd2 39.Rxd2+ cxd2 40.Qxd2 mate. 38...cxd2 39.c3 mate Piece of cake! Emanuel Lasker Without error there can be no brilliancy. 348 The Woodpecker Method

Rxe6 33.Rg7+ Kc6 34.Nd4+! Kc5 35.Nxe6+! Bxe6 36.Rc7+! Kd4 37.Qg1+! title: Lasker – Molina, Buenos Aires (simul) 1910
solution: Emanuel Lasker – L. Molina, Buenos Aires (simul) 1910 24.Qxf7+! 24.Bxf7+? Kh8–+ 24...Qxf7 A much tougher defence is: 24...Rxf7 25.b8=Q+ Kh7 26.Bxf7 Qxf7 27.Rd1!! The only way to defend against the perpetual, but you don’t need to see that in advance – since every alternative to taking on f7 leads to a worse position. 27... Qa2+ 28.Ke3 (28.Ke1 is more passive, but also better for White) 28... Qc2 29.Rd2! Qc1 30.Qxe5! Qe1+ 31.Re2 (31.Kf3 Qxd2 32.Qxc5 is not as good) 31...Qc1+ 32.Kd4 Nb3+ 33.Kc4± White is finally out of danger of a perpetual, but it is not clear that he is winning after 33...Qa3!. 25.Bxf7+ Kh8 25...Kxf7 26.Rf1+ Ke7 27.Rxf8 Kxf8 28.b8=Q++– 26.Rb1! White is winning in several ways, but the most efficient is the game continuation: 26...Rb8 27.Be8! Rxb7 28.Rxb7 Nxb7 29.Bxc6 1–0 Black is simply two pawns down.

title: Capablanca – Pagliano/Elias, Buenos Aires 1911
solution: Jose Raul Capablanca – Pagliano/Elias, Buenos Aires 1911 Black’s king seems to be in serious danger, but with accurate play it can be saved, with a winning material advantage. 27...Bxc3! 28.Bxc3 Nb4+! The game continued 28...Nxc3? after which 29.Qxc3! would have given White a mating attack. Instead it took additional mutual mistakes before White won (1–0, 51 moves). 29.Kb1 29.Bxb4+ Kxb4–+ 29...c5!! With the last black minor piece joining in, White is lost. 29...Rhf8?! 30.Bxe5 Rxf3 31.gxf3 and Black has more than enough for the exchange. It’s far weaker than the main line, but still gives full points.

title: Fernandez Coria – Capablanca, Buenos Aires 1914
solution: Valentin Fernandez Coria – Jose Raul Capablanca, Buenos Aires 1914 16...Bh3! 16...Nxg2 17.Kxg2 Bh3+ looks strong, but there is no win after 18. Kg3µ. 17.Ne3 17.g3 loses an exchange, and even worse is: 17.gxh3 Qg5+ 18.Kh1 Qg2 mate 17...Bxg2–+ 17...Nxg2 18.Nxg2 Qf3 is also good: 19.Ne3 Rd6 with mate. 18.Nf5 The point is 18.Nxg2 Qg5 19.f3 Nh3+–+ picking up the queen on d2. 18...Bxe4 19.Ng3 Nh3 mate Jose Raul Capablanca In chess, as played by a good player, logic and imagination must go hand in hand, compensating each other. 349Solutions to Advanced Exercises

title: T ereshchenko – Alekhine, St Petersburg 1909
solution: Nikolay T ereshchenko – Alexander Alekhine, St Petersburg 1909 20...Ngf4! 21.gxf4 Black does not win material after 21. Kg1 Nxd3 22.Nxd3, but exchanging the light-squared bishop allows him to open files for the rooks with 22...f5 23.exf5 Qxf5µ. 21.Bc2 is more critical. If White gets time for 22. Rg1, Black would have nothing better than retreating with the knight. Fortunately, Black can use the momentum: 21... Nxg3+ 22.Qxg3 Qxf1+–+ 21...gxf4 22.Bd2 Rg8! Threatening 23...Ng3+ and then taking the rook with a discovered check. Both 22... Bh4 23.Qg2 Ng3+ 24.Kg1 Qxg2+ 25.Nxg2 Nxf1 26.Kxf1 and 22...Ng3+ 23.Kg1 Nxf1 24.Bxf1 give unusual piece configurations, with three minor pieces against two rooks. It looks unclear in both cases. 23.Ng2? 23.Rg1 was the only move. 23...Ng3+! 24.Rxg3 fxg3 25.Qg2 Qxh2+ 26.Qxh2 gxh2 27.Kxh2µ And compared to the previous lines, Black has “exchanged” his pawn on f4 for White’s h2-pawn. That gives a passed pawn, and the possibility of exchanging bishops with ...Bg5. 23...Bh4 Or 23...Ng3+ 24.Kg1 Bh4–+. 24.Nd1 24.Nxh4 Ng3+ 25.Kg1 Nxf1+–+ 24...Bxf2 25.Rxf2–+ Three pieces for a queen and a rook is a different story! (0–1, 30 moves)

title: Alekhine – Gutkevitsch, Moscow (simul) 1910
solution: Alexander Alekhine – Gutkevitsch, Moscow (simul) 1910 14.Bh6! 14.Nxg7 Kxg7 15.Bh6+ Kh8µ 14...Ne8 14...gxh6 15.Qxh6 is mating and 14...g6 15.Ng7!+– is winning – it is much better to trade minor pieces on e6 before collecting the exchange. 15.Bxg7! An important move – otherwise 14.Bh6 makes no sense. 15...Nxg7 16.Qh6+– Again the double mate threats on g7 and h7 decide.

title: Fridlizius – Alekhine, Stockholm 1912
solution: Joel Fridlizius – Alexander Alekhine, Stockholm 1912 32.Nf6+! gxf6 33.exf6 White captures on g6 if the queen moves, so Black’s moves are forced: 33...Bxf4+ 34.Qxf4! Qxe1 34...Nxf4+– and White wins the d4-pawn after capturing on e7. 35.Nxg6! Not 35.Qh6? Qe5+ 36.Kh1 Qxf6–+. 35...Qe4 36.Ne7+! Setting up a mating attack, and White could also get a winning position by regaining the exchange at some point. 36...Kh8 37.Rxd4! Mate is unavoidable. The game finished: 37...Qh7 38.Qh4 Rc4 39.Bxc4 dxc4 40.Qxh7+ Kxh7 41.Rh4 mate

title: Fleissig – Alekhine, Bern (simul) 1922
solution: P . Fleissig – Alexander Alekhine, Bern (simul) 1922 19...Nh3+! 20.Kf1!? 20.gxh3 Bxf3–+ forces White to take on f3 to avoid being mated. 20...Qh4 20...Qh6–+ defends the h-pawn and prepares to make use of the pin with ... Ng5. It is also winning, but not as forcing as the text move. However, Black should avoid: 20... Ng5? 21.Qd3! Bxf3? 22.Rxf3!± 21.Qe2 21.Nxh4 Rxf2 mate 21...Qh5–+ There is no defence against 22...Ng5 or 22... Nf4 followed by 23... Nxg2. Also strong is 21... Bxf3 22.Rxf3 Nf4!–+ picking up the h2-pawn with a continuing attack.

title: Grünfeld – Alekhine, Karlsbad 1923
solution: Ernst Grünfeld – Alexander Alekhine, Karlsbad 1923 31...Nf4! 32.exf4 Qc4! The threat against the knight on a2 decides, since White cannot take the queen. 33.Qxc4 Rxd1+ 34.Qf1 34.Kf2 bxc4–+ 34...Bd4+! 35.Kh1 Rxf1 mate Alexander Alekhine Playing for complications is an extreme measure that a player should adopt only when he cannot find a clear and logical plan. 350 The Woodpecker Method

title: Alekhine – Correia Neves, Estoril (simul) 1940

title: Euwe – Felderhof, Netherlands 1931
solution: Max Euwe – William Felderhof, Netherlands 1931 26...g5! 27.Nxe6 27.Rxd8 Rxd8 28.Nxe6 Rd2! is an important move, with a) 29. Qxd2 Qxe4 mate ; b) 29. Qb1 Rd1! 30.Qxd1 Qxe4 mate ; c) 29. Qc4 Rd4! 30.Nxd4 Qxe4 mate . Relatively best is 27.Ng2 when Black can take back the pawn with 27... Rd3+ 28.Ke2 Qxe4+ 29.Kf1 c4µ or win a pawn with 27...fxe4+ 28. Ke2 Qxb5+µ. 27...Rd3+! 28.Kg2 28.Qxd3 fxe4+–+ wins the queen. 28...Qxe4+ 29.Kf1 Rxd1+ 30.Qxd1 Qxe6–+ Max Euwe Alekhine’s real genius is in the preparation and construction of a position, long before combinations or mating attacks come into consideration at all. title: Botvinnik – Batuyev, Leningrad 1930
solution: Mikhail Botvinnik – Andrey Batuyev, Leningrad 1930 18.Nxf7! Rxf7 18...Kxf7 19.Bxe6+ (19.Qxe6+?! Kg6± looks good, but there is no straightforward line) 19...Ke8 20.d5 And there is only one way to stop d5-d6: 20...Rxc3 21.Qb5+! Nd7 22.Rxc3+– Now there is none. 19.Qxe6 Qf8 Black has two alternatives: a) 19...Ned5 20.Nxd5 Nxd5 (20...Rxc1 21.Nxf6++– is an intermediate capture with check) 21.Rxc8+– (or 21.Bxd5+– first) b) 19...Qe8 20.Ne4! The only winning move, but not something you have to see in advance, since the sacrifice would have been promising anyway. The idea is to send the knight to d6. 20... Bxe4 21.fxe4+– simply gives White pawns that are too strong. 20.Re1! Less precise is the game move 20. Ne4?! because 20...Rd8± or 20...Ned5! would have put up quite some resistance: 21.Nd6?! Re8!² 20...Ng6 20...Re8 21.Qxf7+ Qxf7 22.Bxf7+ Kxf7 23.Nb5!+– 21.Ne4+– White jumps in with the knight only when Black no longer has the same defence. In order not to lose the full rook on f7, Black will have to give back a piece on d5, leaving White two pawns up.

title: Lilienthal – Smyslov, Leningrad/Moscow 1939
solution: Andor Lilienthal – Vassily Smyslov, Leningrad/Moscow 1939 14.Nxb5!? cxb5 15.Bc7 Qd7 16.Bf5 Nf6!! The game continued: 16... Ne6?! 17.Bxh7+² (½–½, 42 moves) 17.Bxd7 Bxd7! Black gains a third piece for the queen, since White is not in time to evacuate the c-file. However, White can get a second pawn via a few different routes. Here is one: 18.Ba5 Rac8 19.Nc3 b4 20.f3 bxc3 21.Bxc3÷ You have to decide if you prefer this position to a normal first move. The computer claims a small advantage to White, but it often overvalues the queen. Any non-losing first move gives 1 point, and anticipating that Black gets a third piece for the queen is enough for full points, regardless of whether you decided to take on b5 or not.

title: Smyslov – Stoltz, Bucharest 1953
solution: Vassily Smyslov – Goesta Stoltz, Bucharest 1953 11.b4! cxb4 12.axb4 Bxb4 13.Ncd5+! Nxd5 14.Nxd5+ exd5 15.Bxb4+ Kf6 Defending the pawn is suicidal: 15... Ke6? 16.cxd5+ Kxd5 17.g3 Bf5 18.Bg2+ Be4 19.Rd1+ Ke5 20.f4+ Kf5 21.g4++– 16.cxd5± White’s initial sacrifice secured the bishop pair in an open, unbalanced position. Also, Black’s king would rather have been behind the pawns than in front of them (1–0, 46 moves).

title: Smyslov – Stein, Moscow 1969

title: Smyslov – Minic, Kapfenberg 1970
solution: Vassily Smyslov – Dragoljub Minic, Kapfenberg 1970 35.Rf7! 35.b6! is easily winning and also a practical choice, since it’s hard to calculate the variations in the main line. 35...Rxe5 (35...Nxb6 36.Rc7+– with mate) 36.b7 Rae8 37.Rc8+– 35...Qxe5 36.Rf8+! Kg7 36...Rxf8 37.Qxe5++– 37.Qxe5+ Rxe5 38.Rxa8 Black’s passed pawn looks dangerous, but it is possible to neutralize it. However, to steer for this position, you need to see further; note that Smyslov only drew. 38...e3 The slow 38...Re7 allows White to defend with 39.Kf2 e3+ 40.Ke1 Nf4 41.Rc4!+– and the knight has only one check. 39.b6! Easiest. 39.Kf1? Nf4 40.b6 Rb5 41.Re2 was the game, with a draw. White can play for checkmate with 39.Ra7+. It wins, but requires deep calculation. 39... Kg6 40.Rc6+ Kg5 (40...Nf6 41.Kf1+–) 41.Rxh7! White threatens to exchange rooks. If you saw this far, you score full points. 41... Kf4 42.Rh5! One of several winning moves. Black is busted: 42... Re8 43.Rxd5 e2 44. Rc4+ Ke3 45.Rc1+– 39...e2 40.Rxe2 Rxe2 41.b7 Rb2 42.b8=Q Rxb8 43.Rxb8+–

title: Smyslov – Addison, Palma de Mallorca 1970
solution: Vassily Smyslov – William Addison, Palma de Mallorca 1970 35.Qf7! Defending against 35...Rxf3+ and threatening 36.Qh5+ with a mating attack. 35...Qf1+ 35...Rxf7? 36.Ra8+ Rf8 37.Rxf8 mate is easy. 35...Qxh4+!? was a way to force a queen exchange. However, exchanging one of White’s doubled h-pawns for the g-pawn is a positional concession. 36.Kxh4 g5+! 37.Kxg5 Rxf7 and White has good winning chances after 38. Kg6± or 38.Bd5±. One plan is walking the king to the queenside and sacrificing the exchange, because Black is busy taking care of the h-pawn as well. 36.Kg4! 36.Rxf1 Rxf7² looks like a fortress. 36...Qg2+ 37.Kh5 There are no more checks. 37...Rg8 37...Rb8 38.Qf5 forces Black to give up a pawn to exchange queens with 38...g6+ 39. Qxg6 Qxg6+ 40.Kxg6+– and 37...g6+ is a worse variant of 35...Qxh4+. 38.f4! The queen cannot stay on the g-file. Smyslov won after 38.Ra8 g6+?! 39.Bxg6 mating. 38.Bd5 Rd8 39.Ra8 is the same. 38...Qe2+ 39.Kg5 Be3 40.h3! Only like so. 40...Bxf4+ 41.Kg6 With the g4-square defended, there is no defence against 42. Qxg8+ Kxg8 43.Ra8 mate.

title: Borisenko – Tal, Leningrad 1956
solution: Georgy Borisenko – Mikhail Tal, Leningrad 1956 17.Nxe6! Qxd1 17...fxe6 18.Qxd7 Nxd7 19.Bxe6++– wins back the piece, with two pawns more. 18.Rfxd1 Rc2 18...fxe6 19.Bxe6+ Kh8 20.Bxc8± White has a rook and two pawns for two knights. In this type of open position, especially with no outposts for them, the knights are much inferior to the rook and pawns. Additionally, White will penetrate with a rook on the c-file: 20... Rxc8 21.Rac1 Rxc1 22.Rxc1 Black would be okay with the king on d7, but as it is, White penetrates with the rook. 19.Bxf6 A reasonable choice is 19. Nxf8 Rxb2 20.Nd7 Nc3! 21.Nxf6+ Bxf6± when White has to give back the exchange. He will be a pawn up in an ending with rooks and opposite-coloured bishops. 19...Bxf6 20.Nxf8! Tal gained a blockade after: 20.Bb1?! Nxf2 21.Bxc2 fxe6 22.Bb3 Nxd1 23.Bxe6+ Kh8 24.Rxd1² 20...Bxa1 21.Rxa1 Kxf8 22.Bd5± Mikhail Tal Quiet moves often make a stronger impression than a wild combination with heavy sacrifices. Qxd1 17...fxe6 18.Qxd7 Nxd7 19.Bxe6++– wins back the piece, with two pawns more. 18.Rfxd1 Rc2 18...fxe6 19.Bxe6+ Kh8 20.Bxc8± White has a rook and two pawns for two knights. In this type of open position, especially with no outposts for them, the knights are much inferior to the rook and pawns. Additionally, White will penetrate with a rook on the c-file: 20... Rxc8 21.Rac1 Rxc1 22.Rxc1 Black would be okay with the king on d7, but as it is, White penetrates with the rook. 19.Bxf6 A reasonable choice is 19. Nxf8 Rxb2 20.Nd7 Nc3! 21.Nxf6+ Bxf6± when White has to give back the exchange. He will be a pawn up in an ending with rooks and opposite-coloured bishops. 19...Bxf6 20.Nxf8! Tal gained a blockade after: 20.Bb1?! Nxf2 21.Bxc2 fxe6 22.Bb3 Nxd1 23.Bxe6+ Kh8 24.Rxd1² 20...Bxa1 21.Rxa1 Kxf8 22.Bd5± Mikhail Tal Quiet moves often make a stronger impression than a wild combination with heavy sacrifices. title: Tal – Koblencs, Riga 1957
solution: Mikhail Tal – Aleksandrs Koblencs, Riga 1957 33.R1h6!! The only move to continue the attack. The threat is 34.Rf6+ gxf6 35.Bh6+. 33...d3? 33...gxh6? 34.Bxh6+ Ke8 35.Qxg8 mate 34.bxc3! 34.Rf6+?? Bxf6–+ 34...d2+ 35.Kd1 Qxc6 36.Rf6+! Rf7 36...gxf6 37.Bh6+ Rg7 38.Bxg7+ Ke7 39.Bxf6+ Kd6 40.Be5+ White’s moves so far have been the only way to win. 40...Kd5 41.Rxa7+– 37.Qxg7+!+– 1–0 Instead, Black should have played 33...Qxc6! straight away, or after taking on b2. 34.Rf6+ gxf6 35.Bh6+ Rg7 36.Bxg7+ Ke7 White has a few ways to make a draw from here. One is: 37.Bxf6+ Kd6 38.Be5+ Kd5 39.Rxa7 Bxb2+ 40.Kb1 (40.Kxb2 is a draw by a small margin: 40...Qc3+ 41.Kc1 Qe1+ 42.Kb2 Black can play for more than a repetition with 42... Qxe5! but after 43.Qxg8 d3+ 44.Kb3! d2 45.Qxc8! Qe3+ 46.Qc3 Qxa7 47.Qxd2+= it is a draw nevertheless.) 40...Qc3 41.Bb8 (not 41.Qh1+? Kxe5–+ or 41.Qxg8? Ba1–+) Moving the bishop threatens to check on e5. 41...Qe1+ 42.Kxb2 Qc3+ 43.Kb1= 33.R1h6 was the only move to draw.

solution: Mikhail Tal – Aleksandrs Koblencs, Moscow 1960 14.Qxe7+! 14.Be5 gives full points if you evaluated this position as at least equal (the engines think that it’s fair compensation). 14...Kxe7 15.Nf5+ Ke8 15...Ke6? 16.Nxg7+ Ke7 17.Bd6+ winning the queen. 16.Nxg7+ Kf8 17.Bd6+ Kxg7 17...Kg8 18.Rg1 Qc3+ 19.Rd2 Qa1+ 20.Rd1 is a draw. 18.Rg1+ Ng4 18...Kh6? 19.Bf4+ Kh5 20.Be2+ with a mating net whatever Black plays: 20...Ng4 21.Rxg4 or 20...Kh4 21.Bg5+ Kxh3 22.Kf1. 19.Rxg4+ Kf6 20.Rf4+ Kg7 ½–½

title: Tal – Koblencs, Riga 1961
solution: Mikhail Tal – Aleksandrs Koblencs, Riga 1961 White has a promising position after a slow move, but can force matters: 24.Be5! Qxe6! The only try. 25.fxe6 Kxg6 26.Rf1! Nh7 26...Rhe8 27.Rxf6++– is hopeless. 27.Bxh8 Rxh8 28.Rf8! A move White must see before playing 24.Be5. 28...Rxf8 28...Nxf8 29.e8= Q++– 29.exf8=Q Nxf8 30.e7 Kf7 31.exf8=Q+ Kxf8 White has an easily winning endgame. 32.Kd1 1–0 354 The Woodpecker Method

title: Donner – Tal, Bled 1961
solution: Jan Hein Donner – Mikhail Tal, Bled 1961 32...f3! 33.Bxf3 Qxg4 White cannot defend the bishop and the mate on g1, so his only chance is a counterattack. 34.Nf6+! A move that could be an unpleasant surprise if you haven’t seen it in advance. 34...Rxf6 35.Qe8+ Kh7! 35...Kg7? 36.Bh6+! Kxh6 37.Qh8+ Kg5 38.Qg7+ Rg6 39.Qxg6+ leads to a draw. 36.Qe7+ Qg7 37.Qxg7+–+ The checks are soon over after 37.Qe4+ Kh8 leaving Black with good winning chances. The same evaluation is valid after the game continuation (0–1, 56 moves).

title: Evans – Tal, Amsterdam 1964
solution: Larry Evans – Mikhail Tal, Amsterdam 1964 38...f5+! 38...h5+? 39.gxh6 f5+ 40.Kxf5 Qf3+ 41.Kg5 Qf6+ uses the same motif as in the game, but White can use the extra h-pawn and draw after 42.Qxf6 gxf6+ 43.Kxf6 Rxb8 44.h7+ Kxh7 45.d6. Now Black has only one move that draws: 45... Rf8+! 46.Ke7 Rf1 47.d7 Re1+= 39.gxf6 h5+! 40.Kxh5 Qf3+ 41.Kg5 Qxf6+ The lines are shorter after 41...Qg2+! 42.Kf5 (42.Kh5 Kh7 [or 42...Rxb8–+] 43.fxg7 Re5+ 44.Qxe5 Qg6 mate) 42...g6+ 43.Kf4 Qh2+–+ winning the queen. 42.Qxf6 gxf6+ 43. Kxf6 Rxb8 44.Ke7 Rb7+! 45.Ke8 Rh7 46.d6 Rxh4 47.d7 Re4+ The rook can reach the e-file in several ways and all are equally good. 48.Kd8 Kf7 49.Kc7 Rc4+ 50.Kb6 Ke7–+

title: Tal – Brinck Claussen, Havana (ol) 1966
solution: Mikhail Tal – Bjorn Brinck Claussen, Havana (ol) 1966 34.Ra8! Bxa2? T wo alternatives: a) 34...Rxa8! 35.Bxd5+ (or 35.Qxd5+± which is good, even though White has to worry about a dark-square blockade) 35...Kf8 36.Bxa8± Black should try to use the h-pawn to open White’s king position, but first he must worry about his own. b) If Black starts with 34...Qc1+ 35.Kg2 there is no check on c7 after 35...Bxa2 36.Rxd8+ Kf7. White’s best is 37.b3!, threatening a check on d5. After 37... Qe1! 38.Rd7+! Ne7 39.d5! Ke8! 40.Rd6!, White threatens 41.Rxb6 and 41.Re6 followed by 42.d6. He should be winning. 35.Rxd8+ Kf7 36.Qc6! Ne7 The only defence against the mate on e8. 37.Qe8+ Ke6 38.Rc8! 38.Qd7+ Kf7 39.Rc8 Qd2 40.Qe8+ transposes. 38...Qd5 38...Qd2 39.Rc6+! Kf5 40.g4+! Kxg4 41.Qxe7+– The point of sacrificing the g-pawn is that Black does not have a check on h5 after 41...Qd1+ 42.Kh2!. 39.Rc3+– Or 39.Rc7+–. Black is occupied trying (and eventually failing) to defend, and cannot create any counterplay (1–0, 45 moves).

title: Tal – Gurgenidze, Alma-Ata 1968
solution: Mikhail Tal – Bukhuti Gurgenidze, Alma-Ata 1968 21.Rxh7! Qxe5?! The best defence is 21...Bg7! 22.Bf6! Bxf6! (22...Nxf6 23.exf6 Kxh7 24.Rh1+ Kg8 25.Qh4 with mate) 23.exf6 Nxf6 since White does not get time to sacrifice the bishop on g6. 24.Qxg6+ fxg6 25.Rxc7 ± White wins a pawn on c6 or g6 with good winning chances. 22.Rxf7! Kxf7 Black’s king does at least escape after 22...Bh6! 23.Bxh6 Kxf7 24.Bxg6+ Ke7 25.Bxe8 Rxe8+–, but again at the cost of a pawn and a positional minus. 23.Bxg6+! Kg8 23...Kxg6 24.Bf4++– wins the queen. 24.Bxe8+– Black cannot take back, since White still threatens a discovered check (1–0, 34 moves). 355Solutions to Advanced Exercises

title: Tal – Schmidt, Porz 1982
solution: Mikhail Tal – Bodo Schmidt, Porz 1982 39.Nxf7! 39.Bxg6? fxg6 40.Nfxe6+ looks tempting, but Black has 40...Kg8 41.Rxf8+ Qxf8 and the knight is pinned, forcing White to find the clever 42. Nh7! Rxh7 43.Qxg6+ Rg7 44.Nxf8 Rxg6 45.Nxg6 to be only clearly worse. 39...Rxf7 39...Qxf7 40.Nh5++– White takes the queen and then crashes through on g6. 40.Nxg6! Rxg6 41.Qxg6+ White picks up the h4-pawn and will be at least clearly better, although that evaluation is not so easy to make. 41...Kf8 42.Rxf7+ Qxf7 43.Qh6+ Qg7 43...Ke7 loses to 44.Bg6+– and 45.Qxh4+. 43...Kg8! is best, since the king keeps control over the h8-square. White is winning on the kingside after 44.Qxh4, but Black has some hope to get the d4-pawn. 44...Qe7!± tries to exchange the defender. 44.Qxh4+– 356 The Woodpecker Method

title: Kasparov – Tal, Brussels 1987
solution: Garry Kasparov – Mikhail Tal, Brussels 1987 21.Nxg7! There are a lot of alternatives, but none are as strong: a) 21.Qg3?! Qg5! 22.Rg4 Qe3+² b) 21.Rg4 g5! 22.fxg6 Bxg4 23.gxf7+ Nxf7 24.Nf6+ Kg7 25.Nxg4± c) 21.f6?! g6² 21...Ne4 The main point is 21...Kxg7 22.f6+ Kh8 23.Qh4 with a winning attack. 22.Bxe4 22.Rxe4 Rxe4!± and White is a pawn up, but has less of an attack than in the main line. 22...Rxe4 23.f6+– White has won a pawn and Black’s king is quite exposed. title: Spassky – Petrosian, Moscow 1955
solution: Boris Spassky – Tigran Petrosian, Moscow 1955 White is an exchange up and will win back the trapped queen by a rook check on d7. 40.Rd7+! The game was agreed drawn after 40. Qxh7? Nxh7 41.Rd7+ Qxd7 42.cxd7. Opposite-coloured bishops favour the player with an active position, which is Black in this case. He will use his kingside majority and has full compensation after 42...Bg7. 40...Qxd7 40...Nxd7 41.Qxh7+– and the pawn on e5 drops. 41.Rxe5+ If the king moves, White takes on f8 with check, so the following moves are forced. 41...Qe6 42.Rxe6+ fxe6 The queen is still trapped on h8, but will be resurrected by pawn promotion. 43.c7! Rxh8 44.c8=Q White picks up the queenside pawns and should be winning.

title: Andersen – Petrosian, Copenhagen 1960
solution: Borge Andersen – Tigran Petrosian, Copenhagen 1960 20...Nxe4! Using the back rank and the light squares weakened due to White missing his light- squared bishop. 21.Nxe4 Bf5! White would likely have resigned here. Instead 21... Rf1+ was played and brought a swift victory; it should be winning, even against a tougher defence than was played, but the main line is stronger. 22. Kc2 Bf5 23.Qg2 (a better defence is 23.Rxc4 Rc8 24.Qd3 although White is in trouble after 24... Ra1!–+) 23...Qh4 (or 23...Qa5–+) 24.Rxc4 Qe1!–+ Black has a winning attack (0–1, 29 moves). 22.Qc2 Qh4! 23.Rxc4 Rac8 White is overloaded. 24.Nf3 Rxc4 25.Nxh4 Bxe4–+ Black is a rook up.

title: Petrosian – Spassky, Moscow (12) 1966
solution: Tigran Petrosian – Boris Spassky, Moscow (12) 1966 Black has put his faith in the rolling e- and f-pawns winning the dark-squared bishop to keep his king out of danger. 31.Nf3! Making room for the crucial minor piece to get out of danger and onto the a1-h8 diagonal. Not 31.Bxe4 fxe3 32.Nf3 Rxf3 and Black is not much worse. 31...exd3 White also wins after other moves: 31...exf3 32.Bd2! followed by 33.Bc3, 31...fxe3 32.Nxe5 and 31...Qf6 32.Bd4 . 32.Qxd3! Instead White went for 32.Nxe5? dxc2 33.Bd4! dxe5 34.Bxe5+ Kh7 35.Rg7+ Kh8, but Black had too much counterplay with the pawn on c2, so White had to make a draw: 36. Rf7+ Kg8 37.Rg7+ Kh8 38.Rg6+ Kh7 39.Rg7+ ½–½ 32...Bf5 33.Qe2 33.Nxe5 (33.Bd4 Bxd3 34.Nxe5 transposes) 33...Bxd3 34.Bd4! also wins: 34...dxe5 (34...Be4+ 35.Nf3+!+–) 35.Bxe5+ Kh7 36.Rg7+ Kh8 37.Rxc7+ Kg8 38.Rg7+ Kh8 39.Rxa7+ Kg8 40.Rg7+ Kh8 41.Rg3+ Kh7 42.Rxd3+– All the pawns for the exchange will decide. 33...fxe3 34.Nxe5 exf2 35.Rg2 35.Rf1 is also good. 35...Be4 36.Ng6+ Bxg6 37.Rxf2+– 358 The Woodpecker Method

title: Larsen – Petrosian, Santa Monica 1966
solution: Bent Larsen – Tigran Petrosian, Santa Monica 1966 24.Qh6! Threatening 25.Bxe6 or 25.Rh3. 24.Rxf6? exf6µ gets White nowhere. 24...Bg7 25.Qxg6!! 25.Qh4? is not even a repetition: 25...f5 µ 25...Nf4 a) 25...Nc7 is a double threat, but Black gets no time to execute it: 26.Qxg7+! Kxg7 27.Rg5+ Kh6 28.Rh3 mate b) 25...fxg6 26.Bxe6+ Kh7 (26...Rf7 and White can transpose to the main line with 27.Rxf7 or get a winning attack after 27.Bxf7+ Kf8 28.Bxg6+ Bf6 29.Rh5) 27.Rh3+ Bh6 28.Bxh6 Rf5 29.Rxf5! gxf5 30.Bf7!+– The threat of 31.Bf8 mate is hard to defend against. White could have captured the f5-pawn first, but there’s no point. 26.Rxf4! fxg6 27.Be6+ Rf7 27...Kh7 28.Rh4+ is the same as 25...fxg6 26.Bxe6 Bh6. The only difference is that Black can try 28...Bh6 29.Bxh6! g5 when both moves win: 30.Bxg5++– and 30.Rxg5 Qb6+ 31.c5!+–. 28.Rxf7+– It’s over. Also strong is: 28.Bxf7+ Kf8 29.Bxg6+ Bf6 30.Rh5+– 28...Kh8 28...Be5 29.Rf5+ Kh8 30.Rfxe5+– 29.Rg5! b5 30.Rg3 1–0

title: Spassky – Petrosian, Moscow (5) 1969
solution: Boris Spassky – Tigran Petrosian, Moscow (5) 1969 28.Nc6! 28.Qe5!? maintains a serious advantage. 28...Qd6 29.Qxd6 Nxd6 30.Rc7! and White is probably winning. But 28.Re8? Qxd4–+ should be avoided. 28...Nd6 29.Nxd8! a) Just as good is: 29.Ne7+! Kh8 30.Ng6+! Kg8 (30...fxg6 31.Qxf8+ Rxf8 32.Rxf8+ Kh7 33.d8=Q+–) 31.Nxf8 Nxf5 32.Rxd8 Qxd8 33.Re8+– White enjoys an extra rook after spending a tempo to create luft for the king. b) 29.Rxd8 Rxd8 30.Nxd8 Nxf5 and White only wins an exchange. However, that’s enough after the precise 31. Nb7! Kh7 32.d8=Q Qxb7 33.g4!+– when the knight is caught. 29...Nxf5 30.Nc6 1–0 White queens with an extra rook left on the board. 30. Nb7 would have been similar.

title: Petrosian – Spassky, Moscow (8) 1969
solution: Tigran Petrosian – Boris Spassky, Moscow (8) 1969 34...Rxd3! Black is clearly better and probably winning after simple moves, such as 34...a3 or 34...R3c4, but no points for such cowardice this time! 35.Rxd3 Qxf2+ 36.Kh2 36.Kh1 Ng3+ 37.Kh2 Nf1+ 38.Kh1 Nxe3 is straightforward. 36...Qg3+ 37.Kg1 Material is now equal, but Black wins with a fork on f2. 37...Qf2+ Spassky starts with a repetition. 38.Kh2 Qg3+ 39.Kg1 Nf2!–+ Black captures the pawn on h3, with an ongoing attack. 359Solutions to Advanced Exercises
