title: Marovic – Petrosian, Amsterdam 1973
solution: Drazen Marovic – Tigran Petrosian, Amsterdam 1973 33.Nxe4! 33.Bf3 Be5+! (33...exf3? 34.Nxf3 creates a double threat of Rxg6 and Bxd8. Black is still fine materially, but White’s initiative is winning.) 34.Kh1 Qh6= 33...fxe4 34.Bxe4 Qe6 a) 34...Be5+ 35.Kh1 Qe6 threatens mate, so White has to postpone taking on d8. 36. Re3!+– Black can’t defend against 37.Rg6 (or 36.Rg4+–). b) 34...Qh6 35.Bg5! allows the queen to reach h4. After 35... Qe6 36.Qh4! Be5+ 37.Kg2! Black must give back the piece: 37...Qxh3+ 38.Qxh3 Bxh3+ 39.Kxh3+– Black is lacking coordination: the knights are on the edge, the rook on d8 is threatened and the king can come under attack. And White is also a pawn up. c) 34...Qf7 35.Bxd8 Rxd8 and White has a winning attack; strongest seems 36. Rxg7! Kxg7 37.Rf2 Qe6 38.Qc3+ Nf6 39.Qg3+ Ng4+ 40.Qxg4+ Qxg4 41.hxg4 with a winning endgame. 35.Rxg7! The only winning move in a complicated position. The game continuation 35.Re3? was considered strong by Petrosian in his commentary on the game, but with a computer we can see that it is not the strongest continuation: 35...Rde8 36.Be7 Qe5+! (to prevent Qc3+ after ...Bh6) 37.Kh1 Bh6 and things are not so clear. 35...Kxg7 35...Nxg7 36.Bxd8 Rxd8 37.Qh4++– After the king captures on g7, there are different ways to continue the attack, usually leading to a won endgame. However, it’s enough if your intuition evaluated this position as winning. 36.Bxd8 a) 36.Rg2+ Kh8 37.Qc3+ Rf6 (37...Nf6 38.Rg6 Qxh3+ 39.Qxh3 Bxh3 40.Bxf6+ Rxf6 41.Rxf6+–) 38.Bxf6+ Qxf6 39.Rg5+– b) Or first 36. Qc3+ Rf6 37.Rg2+ Kh8 38.Bxf6+ Qxf6 39.Rg5+–. 36...Rxd8 37.Rg2+ Kh8 37...Kf8 38.Bd5! Qxe1 39.Rg8 mate 38.Qc3+! Black is still fine materially, but White’s initiative is winning.) 34.Kh1 Qh6= 33...fxe4 34.Bxe4 Qe6 a) 34...Be5+ 35.Kh1 Qe6 threatens mate, so White has to postpone taking on d8. 36. Re3!+– Black can’t defend against 37.Rg6 (or 36.Rg4+–). b) 34...Qh6 35.Bg5! allows the queen to reach h4. After 35... Qe6 36.Qh4! Be5+ 37.Kg2! Black must give back the piece: 37...Qxh3+ 38.Qxh3 Bxh3+ 39.Kxh3+– Black is lacking coordination: the knights are on the edge, the rook on d8 is threatened and the king can come under attack. And White is also a pawn up. c) 34...Qf7 35.Bxd8 Rxd8 and White has a winning attack; strongest seems 36. Rxg7! Kxg7 37.Rf2 Qe6 38.Qc3+ Nf6 39.Qg3+ Ng4+ 40.Qxg4+ Qxg4 41.hxg4 with a winning endgame. 35.Rxg7! The only winning move in a complicated position. The game continuation 35.Re3? was considered strong by Petrosian in his commentary on the game, but with a computer we can see that it is not the strongest continuation: 35...Rde8 36.Be7 Qe5+! (to prevent Qc3+ after ...Bh6) 37.Kh1 Bh6 and things are not so clear. 35...Kxg7 35...Nxg7 36.Bxd8 Rxd8 37.Qh4++– After the king captures on g7, there are different ways to continue the attack, usually leading to a won endgame. However, it’s enough if your intuition evaluated this position as winning. 36.Bxd8 a) 36.Rg2+ Kh8 37.Qc3+ Rf6 (37...Nf6 38.Rg6 Qxh3+ 39.Qxh3 Bxh3 40.Bxf6+ Rxf6 41.Rxf6+–) 38.Bxf6+ Qxf6 39.Rg5+– b) Or first 36. Qc3+ Rf6 37.Rg2+ Kh8 38.Bxf6+ Qxf6 39.Rg5+–. 36...Rxd8 37.Rg2+ Kh8 37...Kf8 38.Bd5! Qxe1 39.Rg8 mate 38.Qc3+! Qf6 38...Nf6 39.Rg6 Rf8 (39...Qxh3+ 40.Qxh3+ Bxh3 41.Rxf6!+–) 40.Rh6+ Kg7 41.Rh7+ Kg8 42.Qg3+ Ng4+ 43.Qxg4+ Qxg4 44.hxg4+– 39.Rg5! Qxc3 40.Rxh5+ Kg7 41.bxc3+–

title: Petrosian – Balashov, Soviet Union 1974
solution: Tigran Petrosian – Yuri Balashov, Soviet Union 1974 21.Qe4! Bringing the queen into the centre to attack the light squares (g6 and e6). Not 21.Bxf7+? Kxf7 22.Qc4+ Kg7µ. 21...Kg7 21...Bxg5 22.Qxg6+ Kf8 23.Qxg5+– 22.Bxf7! Kxf7 23.Bh6! Cutting off the king’s retreat, threatening Qe6/c4/d5+ with a devastating attack. 23...Qd6 a) 23...Nd4 defends against queen checks, but White is easily winning after 24.Qxd4. b) 23...Bf6 24.Qc4+ Re6 25.Qxe6 mate c) 23...Nd8 24.Ne5+ with mate. 24.Qc4+! Kf6 White’s attack is so strong that several moves win. 25.Rad1 25.Ng5!+– with threats against f7 and h7. 25...Nd4 26.Qxd4+ Qxd4 27.Rxd4+– Rc5 28.h4 1–0

title: Hübner – Petrosian, Biel 1976
solution: Robert Hübner – Tigran Petrosian, Biel 1976 25.Nf6+! Bad are 25.Bxd5? Rxd5 26.Rxd5 Nb4–+ and White cannot play 27.Rc5, and 25.Rxd5?! Rxd5 26.Bxd5 Nb4 27.Bc4 Nd3µ. 25...Kh8 25...Bxf6? 26.exf6 Qxf6 (26...Qf8 27.Rxd5 Rxd5 28.Bxd5 Nb4 and the difference compared to the immediate capture on d5 is that the bishop on b7 is undefended: 29.Bxb7! Rxc1 30.Rxc1+– White will win the queen back, with an extra piece.) 27.Bxd5 Rxd5 28.Rxd5 Nb4 29.Rc5 With the queen no longer on e7 this defence is possible, with a winning material advantage. 26.Nxd5 White is clearly better, although Black won the game (0–1, 41 moves).

title: Fedorowicz – Petrosian, Hastings 1977
solution: John Fedorowicz – Tigran Petrosian, Hastings 1977 23.Rxf7! Thanks to some nice geometry, White picks up some material and a good position. 23.Qxg6 Nxc3 24.Nxd6+ Bxd6 25.Rxd6 Ne2+ 26.Kd1 Ra6 is unclear. 23...Rxf7 24.Qg8+ Rf8 24...Bf8? 25.Nxe4 Bxe4 26.Nxd6++– 25.Qxg6+ Kd7 26.Nxe4 Bxe4 27.Qxe4± White has three pawns for the exchange and a safer king (1–0, 38 moves). 360 The Woodpecker Method

title: Ivkov – Petrosian, T eslic 1979
solution: Borislav Ivkov – Tigran Petrosian, T eslic 1979 36.Ne4! Attacking the blocker on f6. Not 36. Nxe6? Qxe6 37.Bc4 Qxc4 38.Rxc4 Re1 mate. 36...Nd7 White is certainly happy after this retreat, so you don’t have to see further. After 36...Rf7, the way for White to break through is to win the e6-pawn with the bishop. 37. Bc4 (or similarly 37.Nxf6+ Nxf6 38.Bc4) 37...Ng4 (37...Qb2 38.Nxf6+! [38.Bxe6? Ra1 39.Nxf6+ Kh8! 40.Rf1!= with a perpetual] 38...Nxf6 39.Bxe6 Ra1 and White has enough resources to win material and defend against the perpetual: 40. Bxf7+ Kxf7 41.Qxh7+! Ke8 [41...Ke6 42.Re3+ Kd5 43.Qf7+ Kd6 44.Qe7+ Kd5 45.Qe5 mate ] 42.Qxg6+ Kd7 43.Rf1 The queen can come back to c2 to defend against checks.) 38.Qg5! White has too many threats for Black to parry. (38.Qh4?? Qxc4!µ turns the game around, but 38. Bxa2 Nxh6 39.Bxe6+– is good enough.) 36...Nxe4 37.Rf8 mate 37.Qg5! Many moves are winning, for instance 37.Bc4 first or 37.Nc5 going for the f8-square. Ivkov played the slightly cautious 37.h3?! but perhaps it was time trouble, and the win was spoiled a few moves later. 37...Rf7 38.Bc4 Qb2 39.Bxe6+–

title: Vvedensky – Spassky, Leningrad 1952
solution: Mikhail Vvedensky – Boris Spassky, Leningrad 1952 27.Nxe4! Not 27.Qxe3? Qxh4+ 28.Kg2 Bxf4–+, nor 27.Rxg7? Rxf4–+. 27...Rg6 The point of the knight sacrifice is that White threatens mate after 27...Rxe4 28.Rxg7. Black can try 28...Qxg7 29.Rxg7 Kxg7 but is mated after: 30. Qg1+! (30.Qg3+ also wins, but allows 30... Kf7 31.Bxf6 Nf5) 30...Kf7 31.Bxf6 (31.Bh5++– is not as strong, but still good) 31... Kxf6 32.Qg5+ Kf7 33.Bh5+! Kf8 34.Qf6+! Kg8 35.Bf7+ Kf8 36.Bg6+ Kg8 37.Qf7+ Kh8 38.Qxh7 mate. 27...Rxf4 is met most easily by 28.Qxf4 Bxf4 29.Bxg7+ Qxg7 30.Rxg7 since Black can’t take on e4. 28.Nxd6 Vvedensky lost after 28. Rh5? Qxf4! because 29.Qxf4 Rxg1+µ comes with check. 28...cxd6 29.Rh5 The queen is trapped and cannot escape after trading on g1 due to Qxg7 mate.

title: Spassky – Darga, Varna (ol) 1962
solution: Boris Spassky – Klaus Darga, Varna (ol) 1962 21.Nxe6! fxe6 It is difficult to find a clear-cut win, but as Black’s king cannot castle short or long, there should be something. You can actually chose between three winning moves. 22.Qg4! I think this is most clear-cut, but other moves are also winning. a) 22.Qc4 Qb6 23.Qxa4+ transposes to 22.Qxa4+. b) Spassky played 22.Qxa4+ when 22...Qb5 23.Qg4 was similar to 22.Qg4. If Black had defended with 22...Ke7 the best way is 23.Qh4+ Ke8 24.Qg4+– with the same position as 22.Qg4, but without the pawn on a4. It is a little greedy to spend energy on that, but still full points, of course. 22...Qc6 Black has two other ways to try to defend. a) 22...Qe7 deprives the king of its only square: 23.Qxa4+ is mating. b) 22...Rf8 23.Qxe6+ Be7 24.Rxf8+ Kxf8 25.Rd7 wins the queen with a winning material advantage, or 25.Rf1+ with a winning attack: 25...Ke8 26.Qf7+ Kd7 27.Rd1+ Kc6 28.Qe6+ Kc5 29.Rd7+– 23.Qxg7 Rf8 24.Rxf8+ Bxf8 25.Qxh7+– Black has no active moves, and no defence against 26. Qg6+ Ke7 27.Rd6 Qc8 28.Qf6+ Ke8 29.Rxe6+. Boris Spassky A man who is willing to commit suicide has the initiative. 361Solutions to Advanced Exercises

title: Spassky – Zinn, Marianske Lazne 1962
solution: Boris Spassky – Lothar Zinn, Marianske Lazne 1962 24.Nxf7! Kxf7 24...Nxd6 25.Nxd6+– does not win back the exchange straight away (Black can pin the knight), but with 26.Qe5 to come, Black collapses. 25.Bxe6+ Or 25.Rxe6. 25...Qxe6 26.Rxe6 Kxe6 Black has enough material for the queen, and he would be fine if he had time to return his king to safety. But that dream will not come true. It’s fine to evaluate this position intuitively. 27.Qb3+ Ke7 27...Kf6 28.e5+!+– 28.Qg8! 29.Bg5+ is a threat. 28...h6 29.Rd6! Precise, but other moves were also winning. 29...Nxd6 30.cxd6+ Kd7 31.Qf7+ It is also possible to start with 31.Qxg7++–. 31...Kxd6 32.Bf4+ Kc5 33.Qf5++– The rook on c8 is collected.

title: 1049. Larsen – Spassky, Malmo 1968
solution: Bent Larsen – Boris Spassky, Malmo 1968 20...a5! Not a beautiful combination, but that doesn’t make it any less strong! 21.dxe4 Black’s idea is: 21.bxa5 Bb2 22.Qa4 Be2!³ Only like so. Black has serious threats against both d3 and f1. And not 22...Bxc1?! 23.Rxc1 with compensation for the exchange. 21...Be2!µ A precise move, winning an exchange since the bishop coming to c4 spells trouble for the c5-knight due to the undermining of b4 that was commenced by 20...a5!. 21...axb4 22. Qb3 Ra3! 23.Qb1 Bc3 is also advantageous for Black. 22.Qb3 T ougher is giving up the exchange with: 22.bxa5 Bxf1 23.Rxf1 Bb2 24.e5! Bxa3 25.exd6 Bxc5 26.dxe7µ 22...Bc4! 23.Qb1 axb4 24.Bxb4 Bxa2 Weaker is 24...Bxf1 25.Bxf1µ. 25.Nd3 Bxb1 26.Bxd6 Bxd3–+ (0–1, 48 moves)

title: Hodgson – Spassky, Brussels 1985
solution: Julian Hodgson – Boris Spassky, Brussels 1985 26.Nxd6! Judging this as too dangerous to play and instead going for a normal move would be a reasonable practical decision (1 point). 26...e4! 26...Qxd6 27.Qxf5+– is simple. 27.Nxe4! Ne5! 28.Nxc5! 28.Qe2? Nxe4 29.Qxe4 Nxf3+ and Black wins. 28...Qc8 28...Nxd3 29.Nxd7+– White will retain two extra pawns. 29.Qd4! Hodgson played 29. Qe3? and resigned after 29...Nfg4 30.Qd4 Nxh2!. White is mated after 31.Kxh2 Rh5+ 32.Kg1 Qh3. 29...Nxf3+ 30.Rxf3 Rxf3 31.Ne6!² The knight stops Black’s queen from joining the attack. It is so strong that Black most likely should give up an exchange for it, simultaneously destroying White’s central domination. White should remain slightly better. Other moves than 31.Ne6 would make the whole combination unsound, since it would allow Black to attack. 362 The Woodpecker Method

title: Cramling – Spassky, London 1996
solution: Pia Cramling – Boris Spassky, London 1996 Black seems to have the superior position with his active and useful pieces, but White has a trick up her sleeve. 38.Nxf5! Capturing a pawn while defending e3. Not 38. Bxg4 fxg4µ. 38...Nxh3 38...Kxf5 and either rook check will force Black’s king to leave the knight on g4 en prise: 39.Rf2++– or 39.Rd5++–. 39.e4! White threatens 40.Rxd6 and 40.Kxh3, but Black has a trick of his own that he unfortunately seems to have missed as the game ended here. 39...Nf4+! 40.Kh1!= With accurate play, Black can regain one of the pawns and retain an active position. Not 40.gxf4? Ne3+–+. 40...Rb6 41.gxf4 Bb7 42.Re2 Bxe4+ Black seems to have full compensation, but is no longer better.

title: Fischer – Keres, Curacao 1962
solution: Robert Fischer – Paul Keres, Curacao 1962 White wins a pawn by exploiting the weak black king. 25.Rxd8+ 25.Bxc4 bxc4 transposes to the main line (25...Rxd1 26.Bxe6+–). 25...Bxd8 25...Qxd8? gives up the e5-square to the white queen: 26.Bxc4! Bxc4 (26...bxc4 27.Qe5+– ) 27.Nf6+! (27.Qe5? is now met by 27...f6=) 27...Kh8 (27...Bxf6 28.Qe8+ Qxe8 29.Rxe8 mate ) 28.Qe5+– . The most dangerous threat is 29.Bg7+ and the knight is still poisoned. 26.Bxc4! bxc4 27.Qxc4!+– The pawn plus all the weaknesses are enough for a decisive advantage (1–0, 41 moves).

title: Fischer – Celle, Davis (simul) 1964
solution: Robert Fischer – O. Celle, Davis (simul) 1964 20.Nf5+! The sacrifice opens the e-file, but it is not as easy as it may look. 20...gxf5 20...Ke8 21.Ng7++– and 20...Kf6 21.Rd6 gxf5 22.Qxd7!+– wins the queen (but 22. Rxe6+?! Bxe6 is not so clear). 21.exf5 Rac8 21...Qxf5 22.Qd6+ Kd8 (22...Ke8 23.Rfe1+ Be6 24.Qd7 mate ) 23.Qxf8+ Kc7 24.Qxa8+– 22.Rxd7+! Qxd7 22...Kf6 23.fxe6 (or 23.Qxc8 Rxc8 24.fxe6+–) 23...Rxc7 24.Rxc7+– 23.f6+! 23.Re1+ Ne5! 24.Rxe5+ Kf6 25.Qxd7 Kxe5+– is not as good, but should still be winning (full points). 23...Nxf6 23...Ke8 24.Re1+ mates and 23... Kxf6 24.Qxd7 is over. 24.Re1+ Ne4 25.Rxe4+ Kf6 26.Qxd7 White is easily winning and Black resigned on the next move. solution: Jan Timman – Anatoly Karpov, Montreal 1979 15...Nxh2! 16.c5 A move you should see in advance and make sure you have something against. 16.Kxh2? Qh4+ 17.Kg2 Qh3+ (17...Bh3+ 18.Kh1 Qe4+! 19.f3 Qg6! is also winning) 18.Kg1 Bxg3 Best, but other moves win too by now. 19.fxg3 Qxg3+ 20.Kh1 Re4 21.Rf4 Bh3–+ The attack is overwhelming. 16...Nxf1! Less clear are: a) 16... Be5?! 17.Bxe5 Nxf1 18.Bd4³ b) 16...Bf4!? 17.Qc3 (17.gxf4 Qh4–+) 17...Rxb2! 18.Nxb2 Be5!µ c) 16...Bxg3 17.fxg3 Nxf1µ 17.cxd6 Nxg3! It’s easy to overlook such a move; the fork trick on e2 gives Black a winning advantage with so many pawns and continuing activity. 18.fxg3 18.dxe7 Nxe2+ 19.Kf1 Nxc1–+ 18...Qxd6–+ (0–1, 31 moves) Anatoly Karpov The first great chess players, including the world champion, got by perfectly well without constant coaches. 364 The Woodpecker Method

title: Karpov – Sax, Linares 1983
solution: Anatoly Karpov – Gyula Sax, Linares 1983 Deflecting the queen from her consort’s defence. 35.Re7! 35.Qa8+ Qb8 gets White nowhere but 35.Re4 gives a clear advantage. 35...Rd1+ 35...Qxe7? 36.Qa8+ Kc7 37.Qa7+ Kd8 (37...Kc8 38.Qxe7+– ) 38.Qb8 mate 36.Kxd1 Qxe7 36...Rd8+ 37.Rd7 (or 37.Bd7+, but not 37.Kc1?! Qxe7± and Black’s king has the d6-square) 37...Rxd7+ 38.Bxd7+ Qxd7++– And two pawns up is enough to win. After the game move, you must make sure that you are satisfied with one continuation. 37.Qa8+ Kc7 38.Qa7+ Kd6 39.Qb6+ 1–0 White mates after 39... Ke5 40.Qd4+ Ke6 41.Bb3 mate.

title: Winants – Karpov, Brussels 1988
solution: Luc Winants – Anatoly Karpov, Brussels 1988 The seemingly bad bishop on b2 can become a key attacker. 36.Nc4! Clearing the c1-h6 diagonal. Also full points for similar solutions: 36.Rxg7! Kxg7 37.Nde4! Again, clearing c1-h6. With this move, White protects the f6-knight, rather than preparing a killing Ba3. 36.Nde4! is similar to 36.Nc4 and 36.Rxg7. But do not play like in the game: 36.Ba3? Qxa3 37.Nxd7 Nb5= 38.Nf6? Qa1+–+ Good for a clear advantage is 36.Nh5. 36...Nxf6 36...dxc4 37.Rxg7! Kxg7 38.Bc1 Nxf6 (38...Rh8 39.Qg3+ Kf8 40.Bxh6+! Rxh6 41.Qg8 mate) 39.Qxh6+ Kg8 40.exf6 Qf8 41.Qg5+ Kh8 42.Qh5+ Kg8 43.Bh6!+– And the bishop manoeuvre to g7 decides the game – a much better use than sacrificing itself for a mere knight. 37.Ba3! Qd7 38.exf6+–

title: Karpov – Kramnik, Monaco (blindfold) 1997
solution: Anatoly Karpov – Vladimir Kramnik, Monaco (blindfold) 1997 22...Ne4! 22...Ng4 23.Rg2 and the knight has to retreat. 23.fxe4 23.Rg2–+ drops the f3-pawn. 23...Rxf2 24.Kxf2 Qxh2+ The position can be evaluated as generally winning, due to White’s horrible coordination, so you don’t need to see further. 25.Ke1 25.Kf1 Qh1+ 26.Kf2 Rf8+ mates. 25...Rf8!–+ Kramnik played 25... Qxg3+ 26.Kd2 d4? (The tricky 26... Rc8! also seems to win. Serious kudos if you could evaluate this position as winning!) 27. Kc2 Qg2? (27...d3+=) 28.Nc3 d3+ 29.Kb1+– White was winning, even though the game ended 0–1. After the better 25th move, Black prepares 26... Nf3+ 27.Bxf3 Rxf3, mating. There is no way out, as 26.Kd2 Nc4+ 27.Kd3 dxe4+ picks up the bishop on e2 with a winning advantage.

title: Aronian – Karpov, Hoogeveen 2003
solution: Levon Aronian – Anatoly Karpov, Hoogeveen 2003 27.Be7! Qc7 The bishop can’t be taken: 27...Rxe7 28.Rd8++– And 27...Nc6 28.Bxf6 gxf6 29.Nd7+– sets up forks and a dangerous attack (and 29.Nxc6 is also good enough for a winning advantage). 28.Bxf6 gxf6 29.Qe4! Black cannot defend against the attack without heavy material losses. 29.Ng4+– is also good for White (full points for this too). 29...Ra7 29...Qxe5 30.Qxa8+– 30.Ng4! Kg7 31.Qe3! There are other ways to win as well. 31...Rh8 32.Rd8! 1–0

title: Karpov – Stojanovic, Valjevo 2007
solution: Anatoly Karpov – Mihajlo Stojanovic, Valjevo 2007 22.Qh4! Nxc6 22...h6 23.Nf6! (23.Rg6 Nxc6 24.Rxh6+ is also quite strong, but not clearly winning after 24...Kg8±) 23...Be7 The only move that defends against the immediate mate. There are now three ways to win and you have to have seen one of them to get full points. a) 24.Rxg7 Kxg7 25.Nxe7 Rxe7 26.Nh5+ Kf7 27.Qf6+ Ke8 28.Qh8+ Kd7 29.Nf6+ Kd6 30.Qxc8+– b) 24. Nxe7 Rxe7 25.Rxg7 transposing to 24. Rxg7 (or 25. Ng8 Qxg8 26.Qxe7+–). c) 24.Ne5! Bxf6 25.Nf7+ Kh7 26.Qh5 with a winning attack. 23.Nf6!! h6 23...gxf6 24.Qxf6+ Bg7 25.Qxg7 mate 24.Qxh6+! gxh6 25.Rg8 mate 365Solutions to Advanced Exercises

title: Kasparov – Korchnoi, London (1) 1983
solution: Garry Kasparov – Viktor Korchnoi, London (1) 1983 33...Rxd4 34.cxd4 Nxa4! 35.Rxa4 35.Bxa4 b5–+ 35...Rxb5 36.Ra7+ Kd6!µ Black has good winning chances and won the game. Less strong is the passive 36...Kf6?!³. Endgames are generally more about activity than protecting some irrelevant pawn on the wing.

title: Kasparov – Conquest, London/New York (simul) 1984
solution: Garry Kasparov – Stuart Conquest, London/New York (simul) 1984 24.Nb7! White diverts the black knight from its control over the e4-square. a) 24.Nb3? has the same idea, but allows Black a few checks with the knights: 24...Nxb3 25.Re4 Nc1+ 26.Ke3 Nc2+ 27.Kf2 Nd3+ 28.Kg3 Bh7 And now Black is better, since he protects the e5-square. b) 24.f4!? threatens mate, but after 24... Kxf4 25.Rf3+ Ke4 there is nothing killing, though White has strong compensation. c) 24.Re5+? Kf4 25.Rxc5 Nd3!³ and Black threatens both rooks – the one on h1 with 26...Rhe8+ 27.Kd2 Nf2+. 24...Rd4 24...Nxb7 25.Re4! and mating after 25...Bh7 26.Bh3+ Kg6 27.Ne5 mate. 25.Kf2! Or 25.f4 Kxf4 26.Rf3+ Ke4 27.Nxc5+ Kd5 when White doesn’t win a piece, but gets an exchange with 28.Na5 Kxc5 29.Nb3+ Kd5 30.Nxd4+–. 25.Nxc5?! Rxc4 26.Kf2 Rxc5 27.Re4 threatens mate, but White only has a positional edge after 27...Bh7 28.Rxb4±. 24...Rxc4 25...Nxb7 26.Kg3! Bh7 27.Bh3+ Kg6 28.Ne5 is mate. Also fine is 26.Kg3+– as, to start with, Black must give up a rook to protect against mate. 26. Nd6+ Kf4 27.Nxc4± is not as strong.

title: Wegner – Kasparov, Hamburg (simul) 1987
solution: Hannu Wegner – Garry Kasparov, Hamburg (simul) 1987 18...Bxa4 19.Qxa4 Nc3! The double threat of ...Nxa4 and ...Rd1+ picking up the h1-rook forces White to give up the a1-rook. 20.bxc3 Qxc3+ 21.Ke2 Qxa1 With the king on e2, it is Black who would have the initiative even if he had given up the exchange. But being material up, Black is totally winning and the game ended after only two more moves. Garry Kasparov This is the essential element that cannot be measured by any analysis or device, and I believe it’s at the heart of success in all things: the power of intuition and the ability to harness and use it like a master. 366 The Woodpecker Method

title: Beliavsky – Kasparov, Belfort 1988
solution: Alexander Beliavsky – Garry Kasparov, Belfort 1988 Black must defend against a rook invasion on d7. 21...Bh6+! 21...Qc8? 22.Rdd7+– is a complete failure. But 21...g5!? also protects against the attack while maintaining an advantage: 22. Qxg5 (22.Nxg5 Qg6–+) 22...Qg6 23.Qxg6 hxg6µ White may get three pawns for the piece, but still has a long fight ahead (full points). 22.Kb1 22.Qxh6? Qxe7–+ 22...Rd8! Continuing the counterattacking type of defence. 22...Qc6!? is also winning (full points) due to 23.Qxh6 Qe4+ with smothered mate: 24.Ka1 Nc2+ 25.Kb1 Na3+ 26.Ka1 Qb1+ 27.Rxb1 Nc2 mate. But not 22...g5? 23.Rxe8 gxh4 24.Rxa8 Rxa8 25.a3 Nc6 26.Rd6 and White wins back the piece with equality. 23.Rd6 23.Rxe8 Rxd1 mate The game move seems to trap the queen, but it escapes due to the back-rank mate. 23...Qc6! 24.a3 24.Qxh6 Qe4+ with mate. 24...Rxd6 25.exd6 Qxd6! Moving the threatened piece with 25...Nd5µ is less good, but worth full points if you saw it from the starting position. 26.axb4 cxb4 Black is a pawn up, and has the much safer king – so it’s winning. The game finished soon. 27.Qe4 b3 Showing the weakness of the white king. 28.Nd4 Rf4 29.Qa8+ Bf8 0–1 White’s attack is over, and several pieces are hanging.

title: Kasparov – Salov, Barcelona 1989
solution: Garry Kasparov – Valery Salov, Barcelona 1989 23.c6! 23.Qf6!? Rf8 24.Qg7 is almost winning, with the plan of doubling on the e-file. However: 24...dxc5 25.Re3 Rd3! is an important defensive idea that is easy to miss. 26.Rxd3 Qxb6 27.Re1 Qf6 28.Rxe7+ Qxe7 29.Re3 Be4! 30.Qxe7+ Kxe7 31.Rxe4+± White may look winning, but rook endings are tricky. 23...Bxc6 23...Bc8 24.Qf6+– and the pressure on e7 lets White pick up the kingside pawns to start with. (Other moves should also win, for instance 24. Nd5 Bxe6 25.Nxc7+ Kf7 26.Nxe6+–.) 24.Rac1! The pressure on the black bishops forces Black to give back some material, leaving White with a winning attack for little investment. 24...Rd7 25.Nxd7 Or 25.Qe3+–. 25...Qxd7 26.Qc4 1–0 White’s attack is too much for Black to handle.

title: Kasparov – Ivanchuk, Manila (ol) 1992
solution: Garry Kasparov – Vassily Ivanchuk, Manila (ol) 1992 39.f4?! Ke7! and 39.Be2?! Ke7! do not win. 39.Rd7!! Preventing ...Ke7 which would break the pin that is supposed to win a piece. White is threatening f2-f4. 39...g5!? 39...Kg7 40.Bxe6!+– (but not 40.f4? Nc2!= which is a beautiful trick) 40.Be2! Nxe2 40...Re1 41.Bxh5+– Threatening mate and the knight. 41.Rxd1+–

title: Kasparov – Anand, Linares 1993
solution: Garry Kasparov – Viswanathan Anand, Linares 1993 28.e5! 28.Bxf4 Qxf4 gives White a dominant position, but not a winning one. 28...Qf5 a) 28...Qxe5 loses the rook: 29. Bxf7+ Rxf7 30.Rd8+ Kh7 31.Qxf7+– b) 28... Rxd5 29.exf6 Rxd3 30.Qc2 and White wins the knight or exchange and thus gains a decisive material advantage. c) 28...Ne2+ 29.Kh1! Qe7 (29...Qh4 30.e6!+– ) 30.Bxf7+ (30.e6 should be good enough as well) 30... Qxf7 31.e6+– 29.Bxf4 Qxf4 30.e6! White’s initiative is crushing. Weaker is: 30.Rf3?! Qxe5 31.Bxf7+ Kh7± 30...Rd8 30...Re7 31.exf7++– and White has several ways to defend against the back-rank mate. 31.e7 Re8 32.g3 32.Rf3, as in the game, is also good. 32...Qf6 33.Rf3 If this position had been reached, Black could have resigned in good conscience. 367Solutions to Advanced Exercises

title: Kasparov – Short, London (7) 1993
solution: Garry Kasparov – Nigel Short, London (7) 1993 34.Ng4! 34.f6 Nxf6 35.Bc2+ Kg8 36.Qxh6 Re8= The game move prepares: 35.f6 (the threat of 36.Bc2+ forces Black to take) 35... Bxf6 36.Qxh6+ Nxh6 37.Nxf6+ Kg7 38.Nxd7 Rd8 39.Re7!+– 34...Kg7 a) 34...Qd8 35.f6! (35.Bxf7?! Qg5²) 35...Bxf6 (35...Nxf6 36.Bc2+ or 36. Qxh6+ Kg8 37.Bc2+–) 36.Bxf7+– (or the flashy 36.Bc2+ Kg7 37.Re6!+–) b) 34...Bf6 runs immediately into: 35.Qxh6+! 35.Nxh6! Bf6 35...Nxh6 36.Qg5+ Kh7 37.Bc2! (less strong is 37.f6 Bxf2+! 38.Kxf2 Qf5+ 39.Qxf5+ Nxf5 40.Bc2 Kg6 41.g4±) 37...Bf6 (37...f6 38.Qg6+ drops the knight) 38.Qxf6 Re8 39.Re6!! The only move that’s clearly winning. 39...fxe6 40.fxe6++– 36.Bxf7! 1–0 36.Ng4 is also good enough. The game move provoked resignation, as Black is mated after 36...Rxf7 37.Qg6+.

title: Kasparov – Bareev, Novgorod 1994
solution: Garry Kasparov – Evgeny Bareev, Novgorod 1994 a) 35.Rg6+ fxg6 36.Qxg6+ Kf8 37.Qxh6+ is only a draw as long as Black doesn’t voluntarily step into a check from the bishop: 37...Kf7 38.Qg6+ Kf8 39.Bxg5 Nxc5= b) The straightforward 35.Rxh6 Kxh6 36.Bxg5+ Kg7 37.h6+ Kf8 (37...Kg8? 38.Bxd8 Qxd8 39.Qg4++– and White queens) 38. Qh7 does not win: 38... Ke8!= 39.Qg8+? Nf8 40.h7 Rd1+ 41.Kh2 e4+ 42.g3 Qxc5 Defending the knight on f8 and creating a counter-threat against f2. It is Black who wins. (White can improve in this variation with 38.Bh4!, which should win, however it’s very difficult to see and calculate. The idea is to attack g7 and e7 with the queen and promote the h-pawn. Congrats if you saw this!) c) White’s position is very good, so even passing over the move wins! Let’s try 35.g3 and the logical answer 35...bxc5: 36.Rxh6! Kxh6 37.Bxg5+ Kg7 38.h6+ Kf8 39.Qh7 Ke8 40.Qg8+ Nf8 41.h7 Rd1+ 42.Kh2+– And compared to the previous variation, Black’s queen doesn’t have the c5-square. d) But nevertheless, White needs a forceful move to break through: 35.Bxg5! hxg5 36.Qxg5+ Kf8 37.h6 Or 37.c6 Qxd6 38.Qxd8+ Kg7 39.Qxd7+–. 37...bxc5 38.h7 White queens and mates.

solution: Garry Kasparov – Joel Lautier, Moscow (ol) 1994 28.Ng4!! Qe6 28...fxg4 29. Qxe5+ Rxe5 30.Rxe5+– and 28...Rxg5 29.Nxe5 (29.Rxg5?? Qc7–+) 29...Rxe5 (29...Rxh5 30.Rd8+ Ng8 31.Nxf7 mate ) 30.Rxg5+– both give White an extra exchange. 29.Rd8! White threatens mate on g7. 29.Qf6+?! title: Piket – Kasparov, Linares 1997
solution: Jeroen Piket – Garry Kasparov, Linares 1997 39...e3! 39...Bg5 40.Bxg5 Rxg5 41.Rf4 Qxg3 42.Rf8+! leads to stalemate. 40.Re6 The e-pawn decides after 40.Rxh6 e2–+ and 40.Rxd6 e2! (or 40...Bg5 41.Bxg5 Qf3+! 42.Kh2 Qf2+ 43.Qxf2 exf2 44.Rf6 Rf7–+) 41.Rd8+ Kf7 42.Qc7+ Kg6 when White has only a few more checks. 40...Rc7! Kasparov played: 40...Qf3+? 41.Kg1 (41.Kh2?? Qf2+ 42.Qxf2 exf2 43.Rf6 Rf7–+) 41...Rf7 (41... Rxg3+ 42.Bxg3 Qxg3+ 43.Kf1 and Black has only a perpetual) 42. Qg6+ Bg7 43.Re8+ Rf8 44.Rxf8+ This was about equal and ended in a draw. The rook move overloads White’s queen, but White has several moves, including two different checks on g6. a) 41.Qxc7 Qf3+ 42.Kh2 Qg2 mate b) 41.Qe4 Qd1+ (41...Qxe4+ also wins after 42. Rxe4 Rc2–+) 42.Kh2 Rc2+ 43.Kxh3 Qf1+! 44.Kg4 Rc4–+ c) 41.Re8+ Bf8 42.Qe4 And in contrast to the immediate 41. Qe4, Black can’t win by exchanging on e4, but he still has the same pin on c4: 42... Qd1+ 43.Kh2 Rc2+ 44.Kxh3 Qf1+ 45.Kg4 Rc4–+ d) 41.Qg6+ Qxg6 42.Rxg6+ Kh7 (or 42...Bg7–+) 43.Re6 Rc2–+ e) 41.Rg6+ The move that makes it easy to avoid calculating the rook sacrifice on c7. 41...Bg7 41...Kf8 42.Rf6+ Rf7! also wins and gives full points. 43.Rxf7+ (43.Rxh6 Qf3+ [or 43...Rf1+ 44.Kh2 Rf2+–+] 44.Kh2 Qf2+ 45.Qxf2 exf2–+) 43...Kxf7 44.Qc7+ Kg8 45.Qd8+ Bf8 46.Qg5+ Qxg5 47.Bxg5 e2–+ 42.Rxg4 Rxc2–+ White can win the bishop on g7, but it doesn’t help when he has to give up the rook for the e-pawn.

title: Kasparov – Kramnik, Frankfurt 2000
solution: Garry Kasparov – Vladimir Kramnik, Frankfurt 2000 31...Qg4+ is an immediate repetition if Black wants. White can’t run with the king, for example: 32.Kf1 Qh3+ 33.Ke2 Rc2+–+ Kramnik started with 31...Bg5 but soon repeated moves. Note that 32.Nd3 Qxd3? is losing for Black. The attack has slowed down and White has time for 33.a7. But Black should not be satisfied with a draw. 31...Rc5! Preventing the queen from coming home to defend the kingside, and threatening to attack f2 with the queen, or take the pawn straight away. Black can also start with a queen check before the rook move. 32.Nd3 32.Qxc5 dxc5 33.Nc2 Qg4+ 34.Kf1 Qf3–+ and White’s king can’t escape from mate. 32...Qxd3 33.Qxc5 Rxc5–+ Black is material up and just needs to keep enough pressure on the white king to prevent the promotion of the a-pawn. 34.Rb2 34.a7 Bxf2+ and Black wins. 34...Bxf2+ 35.Rxf2 Qd4 36.Ra3 36.Raa2 Rc1+ 37.Kg2 Qd1–+ 36...Rc2 36...Rc7 should also be winning. 37.Raf3 Qa1+ Or 37...Rxf2 first. 38.Kg2 Rxf2+ 39.Rxf2 Qxa6–+ Black should be able to convert.

solution: Garry Kasparov – Yevgeniy Vladimirov, Batumi (rapid) 2001 23.Nh7! Not 23.Nxf7? Bxd5!µ or 23.Ne6+? fxe6 24.Qh6+ Kf7 25.Qh7+ Ke8 26.Qxg6+ Kd8 27.Bxe6 Qe8–+. 23...Bxd5 23...Kxh7 24.Qh6+ Kg8 25.Qxg6+ Kh8 26.Qxh5+ Kg8 27.Re3+– (the rook lift can also be delayed with 27. Bh6+–) 24.Qh6+ Kg8 25.Bg5 After 25.exd5+– (full points), Black must part with an exchange, since 25...Rfd8 26.Bg5 leaves him too exposed. 25...Bxg5 Black resigned after playing 25...Bxe4. 26.hxg5 f5+– White captures on f8 now or after the check on g6. 369Solutions to Advanced Exercises

title: Adams – Kasparov, Linares 2005
solution: Michael Adams – Garry Kasparov, Linares 2005 25...Nc2! 25...Qc2 26.Qxc2 Nxc2–+ is also good, but not immediately winning (1 point). 26.Kb1 One main point is: 26.Nxc5 Rxb2 mate The other point is allowing the queen to come closer to the attack: 26...Qa3 0–1 White had had enough, since there is no defence to Black’s threats: 27.Qxc2 Rfc8 28.Qd2 Qxa4 and the b2-pawn will fall with devastating consequences.

title: Khalifman – Ubilava, Kuibyshev 1986
solution: Alexander Khalifman – Elizbar Ubilava, Kuibyshev 1986 32.Bxf7+! Kh7 32...Rxf7 33.Nxe5 Qf6 34.Qxf7+ (or 34. Nxf7+–) 34...Qxf7 35.Nxf7 Kxf7 36.Rc7++– 33.Rd1± (1–0, 40 moves) Slightly stronger than the game continuation is 33.g4!+–, keeping up the attack; a pawn is only a pawn, but a strong attack can end the game. White is threatening 34. Ng5, thus forcing Black to further weaken his king position by moving the g-pawn. 33...Bxe4 34.Ng5+ hxg5 35.Qh3 mate is one important point.

title: Khalifman – Dolmatov, Minsk 1987
solution: Alexander Khalifman – Sergey Dolmatov, Minsk 1987 30...b5! Weaving a mating net, starting with a threat of 31...b4+ 32.Ka4 Rxa2 mate. 31.Ra1 31.b4 R8c3 mate 31...Bf5! The bishop needs to be rerouted to the e8-a4 diagonal. T o do so with a threat on the rook is of course nice. 32.Rg2 Bxe6 Protecting the d5-pawn on the way! 33.f4 White tries to exchange the rook on c2. 33.Rg6 is met by: 33...Bd7–+ 33...b4+ 33...Rc1 34.Rxc1 Rxc1 is much better for Black, but mate is even better. 34.Ka4 R2c5! The threat of ...Bd7 mate is decisive. Or similarly 34... R8c5–+ or 34... Ra8–+, but not 34... Bd7+ 35.Kxa5 when White picks up the pawn on b4 and Black only has a perpetual.

title: Khalifman – Godena, Vienna 1996
solution: Alexander Khalifman – Michele Godena, Vienna 1996 29.Rxh6+! gxh6 29...Kg8 loses to many things, for instance 30.Rh7 Rf7 31.Bxf6 Qc7 32.Qh5. 30.Qxh6+ Kg8 31.Qg6+ Kh8 32.Bxf6+ Rxf6 33.Qxf6+ Kg8 34.Qg6+ Kf8 34...Kh8 35.f6+– Qc7 36.f7 (or 36.Bc2+–) 36...Rf8 37.Qh6 mate 35.f6! With a winning attack. The game concluded: 35...Qc7 36.Qh6+ Kg8 37.Qg5+ Kh7 38.Qxc5?! 38.Bc2+ is better. 38...Re5? 38...Qe5! would have given Black hope. 39.Qf8 Rh5 40.Bc2+ 1–0 Mate will be delivered. Alexander Khalifman T o make any move in a position, merely so as not to spoil anything – such a purely practical approach is not for me! 370 The Woodpecker Method

title: Kramnik – Schneider, Mainz (simul) 2001
solution: Vladimir Kramnik – Joerg Schneider, Mainz (simul) 2001 35.Qf4! Black can’t defend d6 in a good way. The game instead went 35.e5? Qxe5 36.Qxe5+ dxe5 37.d6+ Ke6 38.Nc7+ Kxd6 39.Nxa8. It’s a forcing line, winning material, but Black can get counterplay with the c-pawn after: 39... Nd5! (which was not played) 40. Ra1© 35...Qe5 35...Rad8 does not help: 36.Nxd6 Rxd6 37.e5+– 36.Qxe5+ dxe5 37.d6+ Ke6 37...Kd7! is a better defence, but 38.Rxf6± still gives White winning chances. 38.Nc7+ Kxd6 39.Nxa8+– The pawn on e4 makes a great difference compared to the game.

title: Akopian – Kramnik, Wijk aan Zee 2004
solution: Vladimir Akopian – Vladimir Kramnik, Wijk aan Zee 2004 29.Rh7!! Qxb2+ White’s main point is 29...Kxh7 30.Nxe7+ Kh6 31.Rh1+ Bh5 32.g4 mating (32.Nf5+ and 32.f4 are also winning). And 29...Nxb2 allows White to collect a piece: 30.Rxg7+ Kf8 31.Qxb2+– 30.Qxb2 Nxb2 31.Rxg7+ Kf8 32.Rh1 1–0 Or 32.Kxb2 e6 and Black gets his piece back, but a pawn and an attack would still be good enough for White to win the game here.

title: Kramnik – Van Wely, Wijk aan Zee 2004
solution: Vladimir Kramnik – Loek van Wely, Wijk aan Zee 2004 37.Rh8! f6? 37...Re3+! 38.Qxe3 (38.Nxe3 seems to be less practical since White's attack is not dangerous. 38...Kxh8 39.Ra8+?! Kg7 40.Ng4 is met by 40...g5 ².) 38...Qxe3+ 39.Nxe3 Kxh8 40.Kxh4+– This is the toughest defence. White still has difficulties to overcome in order to get the full point. Easier is 37... Kxh8 38.Qh6+ Kg8 39.Ra8+ with mate. 38.Qh6+! Instead the game continued 38.Rxh4? Rxh4+ 39.Kxh4 when 39...b4!² would have activated the rook and given Black good chances to hold. 38...Kf7 39.Rh7+! Or 39.Qh7+! Ke6 40.Qxg6+– or 39.Rf1!?+–. 39...Ke6 39...Ke8 40.Qxg6++– 40.Qxg6+– The knight is indirectly protected so White is a piece up, and has very dangerous threats.

title: Nijboer – Anand, Wijk aan Zee 1998
solution: Friso Nijboer – Viswanathan Anand, Wijk aan Zee 1998 17...Rxc3! 18.Bd3 a) 18.bxc3 Nd5 19.Rxd5 (19.Qh3 Nxc3+–+) 19...exd5!–+ The bishop protects h3 (19...Qxd5?? 20.Qh3 is mating). b) 18.Qxc3 Qxc3 19.bxc3 is simply winning for Black, since White no longer has any threats on the h-file. 18...Rxd3 Or 18...Ba4–+. 19.cxd3 Ng4 20.Qh3 Nh6–+ Black defends and wins, since he can afford to give back one piece.

title: Anand – Shirov, Monaco (rapid) 2000
solution: Viswanathan Anand – Alexei Shirov, Monaco (rapid) 2000 22.f6! 22.Qg4 f6² 22...gxf6 23.Bxh7+ Also full points for the following line: 23. Qg4+ Kh8 24.Bxh7 fxe5 25.Qh5! f6 26.Bg6+ (or similarly 26.Bf5+) 26...Qh7 (26...Kg8 27.Rh3!+–) 27.Bxh7+– 23...Kxh7 24.Qh5+ Kg8 25.Qg4+! 25.Rh3 Ne4 leads nowhere. 25...Kh7 26.Bg5! 26.Rhf1! fxe5 27.Nf5!+– is also enough for full points. 26...Rh8 27.Bxf6 Qf8 28.Nf3! Bringing the knight into the attack decides the game. Instead, the game went 28. Qh5+?! Qh6 29.Qxh6+ Kxh6 30.Bxh8 Ne4±, giving Shirov the opportunity to eventually turn things around, and win. 28...Kh6 29.Ng5 Rg8 30.Qf4!+– Viswanathan Anand (on Kasparov’s 1996 match victory over Deep Blue) I’ll take my five positions per second any day, thank you. 372 The Woodpecker Method

title: Anand – Polgar, Leon (advanced 1) 2000
solution: Viswanathan Anand – Judit Polgar, Leon (advanced 1) 2000 24.Re1! Other moves are good enough for an advantage, but pinning the e-pawn steps up the pressure and wins. The threat is to take on f5. Not 24.Nf6+? Bxf6 25.Bxf6 Rxd6±. 24...Rxd6 24...Qf7 25.Bxf5 Rxd6 transposes and 24...exd5? runs into: 25. Rxe8 Qxe8 26.Qg7 mate 25.Bxf5! White threatens to take on g6 and Black can’t defend. 25...Qf7 26.Bxg6! Nxg6 26...hxg6 27.Qh8 mate 27.f5! e5 28.Bxe5?! Better would have been 28.Rxe5! Rxe5 29.Bxe5 Bxd5 30.cxd5 Rxd5 31.Rxg6+ and wins. 28...Bxd5 29.cxd5 Rxe5 30.Rxe5+– White failed to convert his winning advantage.

title: Anand – Bareev, Shenyang (2) 2000
solution: Viswanathan Anand – Evgeny Bareev, Shenyang (2) 2000 32.g4! Preparing to dislodge the king from e6, giving White the needed time to get the pawns sufficiently advanced. 32.b5? Rcd8 33.c6 looks like a tactical solution, but it fails: 33... Rxd5 34.Rxd5 Rxd5 35.c7 Kd7 36.Kxd5 e3!–+ Another inferior option is: 32. Ne3 Rxd4+ 33.Kxd4 Rd8+ 34.Kc4 Rd3µ 32...Rg7 32...Rf7 33.b5+– 33.Ne3 A possible way, but not as good, is 33.h3 h5 34.g5. The idea is that 34... Rd7 35.Rd1 Rcd8 36.c6!± works for White when there is a second passed pawn; White gets a good queen ending. But 33.g5? Rd7! still gives White problems. 33...fxg4 34.Rd6+ 34.Rxe4+ also wins. 34...Kf7 35.Nf5! Winning the exchange, when the queenside pawns and the active pieces will decide. The game ended quickly: 35...e3 36.Nxg7 Re8 37.Nxe8 e2 38.Rf6+ 1–0

title: Karjakin – Anand, Wijk aan Zee 2006
solution: Sergey Karjakin – Viswanathan Anand, Wijk aan Zee 2006 25...Rc8! 26.Qxe7 Nc4! 26...Rxa3? 27.bxa3 Qxa3 (27...Nc4 28.Qa7+–) 28.Qa7!+– After the knight move, an intuitive evaluation that Black’s attack is promising seems reasonable, however there is also counterplay to take care of. 27.g6! 27.Bc5 Rxa3! 28.Bxa3 (28.bxa3 Rxc5! with a winning attack, but not 28...Nxa3+? 29.Kc1! Rxc5+ 30.Kd2 Rc2+ 31.Ke3±) 28...Nxa3+ 29.bxa3 Qxa3 Black’s attack is decisive. 30.Rd2 b2 (or 30...Ra8–+) 31.Rxb2 Qd3+ 32.Ka1 Ra8+ 33.Ra2 Qc3+ 34.Kb1 Rb8+ With mate. 27...hxg6! Black loses after 27...fxg6? 28.f6 and 27... Rxa3? 28.gxf7+ Kh8 29.f8=Q+ Rxf8 30.bxa3. Without the rook on c8, White can defend. 28.fxg6 Nxa3+ Also winning is: 28...Rxa3 29.Qxf7+ (29.gxf7+ Kh7!–+) 29...Kh8 30.bxa3 Nxa3+–+ 29.bxa3 Rxa3 30.gxf7+ Kh7!–+ The point behind exchanging on g6.

title: Bruzon – Anand, Leon 2006
solution: Lazaro Bruzon – Viswanathan Anand, Leon 2006 20.Qh5! Bxe5 20...Nxe5 21.Qxh7+ (or 21.fxe5 h6 22.exd6+–) 21...Kf7 22.fxe5 Rh8 23.exd6 Rxh7 (23...Qd7 24.Qxh8 Rxh8 25.Rxh8+–) 24.dxc7+– 21.fxe5! Not 21.Qxh7+? Kf7 22.fxe5 Rh8–+ or 21.dxe5?! Qb6+! 22.Kh1 Kf7= when Black is ready to capture the knight if it goes to c4. 21...Qxc2 21...Kf7 22.Nc4! The only winning move, protecting against ... Qxc2 and threatening Nd6+ followed by taking on c8. (22.Qxh7? Rh8–+) 22...Rcd8 23.g4+– 22.Qxh7+ Kf7 23.Rg3! 23.Nc4!? Rxc4 is not as clear, and White still needs to find 24.Rg3!±. And 23.Rh6?! Ne7 24.Rf6+ Ke8 25.Qxg7 Rg8!² also fails to win. 23...Qxd2 23...Qxb2 24.Qxg6+ (24.Rxg6? Qxd4+ 25.Kh1 Qxe5–+) 24...Ke7 25.Qg5+! Ke8 26.Qh5+! Kd8 27.Rxg7 Qxd4+ 28.Kh1 Rc7 29.Qh4+ (29.Qg5+ is the same) 29... Kc8 30.Rxc7+ Kxc7 31.Qe7++– Yes, you need to find all these moves to get a winning position (but not before playing the first move). It’s easier after: 23...Rg8 24.Qxg6+ Ke7 25.Bc1+– 24.Rxg6!+– 24.Qxg6+? Ke7 25.Qxg7+? (25.Qh7 Rf7 26.Rxg7 Rcf8=) 25...Rf7µ In the game White concluded his attack in the most efficient way: 24...Rg8 25.Rxe6! Kxe6 26.Qxf5+! Ke7 27.Qf7+ Kd8 28.e6! 1–0 It’s mate on d7. 373Solutions to Advanced Exercises

title: Anand – Carlsen, Nice (blindfold) 2008
solution: Viswanathan Anand – Magnus Carlsen, Nice (blindfold) 2008 The pawn on c7 seems lost, but through powerful play it becomes the star. 27.c5! 27.f3 Rxc7 28.fxe4± 27...bxc5 27...b5?! is simply bad, for instance: 28.a4 bxa4 29.b5+– 28.b5! cxb5 28...Rxc7 29.b6+– 29.Nxb5+– The powerhouse on c7 gives White a winning advantage. After 29...Rxa2 strongest is rerouting the bishop to h3 with 30.Bf1.

title: Mamedyarov – Anand, Khanty-Mansiysk 2014
solution: Shakhriyar Mamedyarov – Viswanathan Anand, Khanty-Mansiysk 2014 26...Ng4! 26...Re2 27.h3³ and Black can’t take on h3. 27.Qc2 27.h4 Ne3 28.Bxe3 Rxe3–+ White’s kingside is falling apart. 27...c5! Driving away one defender or another. 28.Nxc5 28.Bc3 is met by 28...Ne3–+ or 28... Bxc3 29.bxc3 Ne3–+. Nor does 28. Be5 save White: 28...c4! 29.Nd4 Bc5–+ 28...Rc8–+ Black wins a piece on c5. Also working is 28... Bxc5 29.Bxc5 Rc8 followed by ...Rxc5. But note that after 30. Rd1 Black has to start by defending against the back-rank mate: 30...Nf6–+ 374

title: Ponomariov – Short, Madrid 2016
solution: Ruslan Ponomariov – Nigel Short, Madrid 2016 24.Rxg6+! All Black’s minor pieces are on the queenside, so an all-out attack should be considered. Not 24.Bh3? Qf7–+. 24...hxg6 25.Qxg6+ Kh8 White just needs one more piece in the attack, or to get the bishop to f6. 26.Bh3! 26.Bg5 Rf8= 26...Qh7 26...Qe7 27.Bg5!+– (27.Be6 Nxc4 28.Bf7 is also winning) 27.Qf6+ 27.Qxe8+ is also mating, but not as quickly (full points). 27...Kg8 28.Be6+! Rxe6 29.Qf8 mate Ruslan Ponomariov (on how to concentrate) Drinking some water at a critical moment, when your lips are drying out from the tension, can really help. title: Khenkin – Kasimdzhanov, Moscow (4) 2001
solution: Igor Khenkin – Rustam Kasimdzhanov, Moscow (4) 2001 23...Bxb2! Giving up the queen for plenty of other stuff. The alternatives are worse for Black. 24.Rxa5 Bxc3 Both rooks cannot be protected, and White’s counterplay is tamed by Black’s continuing threats. 25.Qxh6 Bxe1! 25...Bxa5? 26.Re5+– (26.Rxe6 Bd2 [26...fxe6 27.Qg6++–] 27.Qxd2 fxe6±) 26.Ra3!? 26.Qxf6? Bxa5–+ is easy, but 26.Rc5 is trickier. Black should play 26...Ne8!µ to protect the king. 26...Bb4! 27.Rb3 Bf8!–+ 27...Be7µ 28.Qxf6? Rc1+ 0–1 Mate is coming.

title: Berelowitsch – Kasimdzhanov, Germany 2005
solution: Alexander Berelowitsch – Rustam Kasimdzhanov, Germany 2005 19.Rxe5! Winning a centre pawn with tempo is often a good idea. 19.bxa5 Rad8 gives Black compensation due to the threats ... Nxe1, ...e5-e4 and ...Bb4 (keeping the pawn). 19...Qd8 19...Nxe5? 20.Qxd5+– ; 19...Qd6 20.Rxa5± 20.Rxe7! 20.Rxa5 Bxb4± is good enough for full points. 20...Qxe7 21.Qxd3+– White’s activity and Black’s misplaced knight on a5 actually gives White a winning advantage. The game nicely illustrates the hopelessness of Black’s position. 21...Qxb4 22.Ng5 g6 23.Rxc3 Qxa4 24.Ba3 Rfe8 25.Qf3 1–0 The knight on a5 falls if the queen retreats to protect f7. Rustam Kasimdzhanov There can also be tactics that do not work, or tactics which are refuted by other tactics. The Path to Tactical Strength (2007) Solutions to Advanced Exercises 376

title: Ubilava – T opalov, Ponferrada 1992
solution: Elizbar Ubilava – Veselin T opalov, Ponferrada 1992 13.Nb5! White does not win any material immediately, but Nd6 followed by Qb3+ is a winning threat. 13...bxc5 13...cxb5? 14.Bxa8+– ; 13...Qe7 14.Nd6+– and such a strong knight will cost an exchange at the very least. 14.Nd6 Or 14.Nc7+–. 14...Qe7 15.Be3!+– Instead the game continued 15.Qb3+? Rf7 (15...c4!=) 16.Nxf7± and White won eventually.

title: T opalov – Illescas Cordoba, Linares 1995
solution: Veselin T opalov – Miguel Illescas Cordoba, Linares 1995 20.Nc7! White creates threats against d6 and e6, and the black bishop can’t hold both d5 and f5. 20...exf4 White is not afraid of a sacrifice: 20...Rxg3+ 21.hxg3 Qxg3+ 22.Ng2+– A better try is 20...Bc4!? 21.Nxf5 (21.Nxc4? exf4! with an initiative) 21...Rxf5, but White seems to be winning after 22.Bxf5. 21.Ng2! Qh3 21...Qe7 22.Nxe6 Qxe6 23.Bb3+– 22.Rxf4! A necessary move to make the combination sound. Instead 22. Nxe6? fxg3 23.hxg3 Be3+! completely turns the tables: 24.Rf2 (24.Nxe3 Qxg3+ 25.Kh1 Qh3 mate) 24...Bxf2+–+ Also misguided is: 22. Nxf4? Bxf4 23.Rxf4 Rxg3+ 24.hxg3 Qxg3+ 25.Kh1 Qh3+ 26.Kg1 Rf6µ 22...Bxf4 22...Rxc7 23.Rh4+– 23.Nxf4 Rxg3+ 24.Kh1!+– Wherever the black queen moves, White can play 25.Ncxe6 with a winning position (and there are also other good moves). 24.hxg3?! may be slightly better for White after 24...Qxg3+ 25.Ng2 Ne5! 26.Nxe6 Nf3+ 27.Qxf3! Qxf3.

title: Carlsen – Nielsen, Malmo/Copenhagen 2004
solution: Magnus Carlsen – Peter Heine Nielsen, Malmo/Copenhagen 2004 32.g6! Opening up for the rook on d5 and queen on e3. 32...fxg6 a) 32...Rxb2+ 33.Ka1 (33.Bxb2?? Qc2+ 34.Ka1 Qxb2 mate) 33... Qxg6 34.Rdh5+– (or 34.Rg5+– or a couple of other moves) b) After the game move 32...f6 White can win in many ways, for instance 33. Rdh5 Kf8 34.Rh8+ Ke7 35.Rxc8 Qxc8 36.Qa3++–, picking up a piece to start with. c) 32...Qxg6 33.Rg5!+– and the attack crashes through on g7, while Black’s attack stalled by bringing the queen to g6 (or 33.Bxg7+– also works). 33.Rh8+! Kxh8 33...Kf7 34.Qf4+ with an attack that mates in several ways. 34.Qh6+ Kg8 35.Qxg7 mate Veselin T opalov There was a moment at the beginning when the machines were a positive, but lately we’ve being passing to the other extreme. Now it seems that a move isn’t good unless the machine says so. Magnus Carlsen Of course, analysis can sometimes give more accurate results than intuition but usually it’s just a lot of work. I normally do what my intuition tells me to do. Most of the time spent thinking is just to double-check. The Woodpecker Method 377

title: Carlsen – Lagno, Lausanne 2004
solution: Magnus Carlsen – Kateryna Lagno, Lausanne 2004 21...g6! Removing the threat on d5. 22.Qh6 22.Qg4 Nxg2–+, or 22...Nxe3–+, or 22...Qxg4 23.hxg4 Nxg2–+. 22...Nxg2! Winning a pawn due to the discovered check. 23.Kxg2 Nf4+! The game continuation 23...Bf8 24.Qh4 Nxe3+ is also winning (0–1, 53 moves). But 23...Nxe3+ 24.Kg1 Bf8 25.Bxf7+!µ is not so clear. 24.Kg1 24.Kf1 Bg5!! 25.Qxg5 Qxh3+ 26.Kg1 Qg2 mate 24...Bg5! 25.Bxf7+ Kh8–+ Black wins the queen.

solution: Peter Svidler – Magnus Carlsen, Moscow (blitz) 2008 37.Qg6! A multipurpose move preparing 38.Rg4, 38.Qxe6+ and 38.Be4. title: Giri – Carlsen, Paris (blitz) 2016
solution: Anish Giri – Magnus Carlsen, Paris (blitz) 2016 21.Nxe6! Rxe7 21...fxe6 22.Rxd7± 22.Nxg7! Qb7!? A double threat against f3 and g7 (since the knight on d7 is protected). 22... Kxg7 23.Rxd7! (the move order 23. Qg4+ Bg6 24.Rxd7 runs into 24...Rxe3 or 24...Qc8) 23...Rxd7 24.Qg4+ Kh8 25.Qxd7 Regaining the rook, when the two healthy pawns extra and his safer king leaves White winning. 23.Bd4!+– Pinning the e4-bishop so that ...Bf3 is not possible while simultaneously protecting the g7-knight. Here too, White is two pawns up for no compensation. 23. Qg4 Bf3 24.Qh4 Rxe3 25.Nf5 is a good try, but Black can defend with 25...Re6 26.Qg5+ Rg6÷ and things are not so clear.

title: Guseinov – Carlsen, Internet (blitz 1.3) 2017
solution: Gadir Guseinov – Magnus Carlsen, Internet (blitz 1.3) 2017 27...Bc2!!–+ Clearing a path to f2 with tempo. Since the c2-square is defended twice, considering 27...Bc2 as a candidate is the difficult part; after that, the variations are not so difficult to calculate. a) 27...Bg6 is slow by comparison, but still gains an advantage. For example: 28.gxf4 Qxf4 29.Qe2 Qxd2 30.Qxd2 Bxd2µ b) 27...Nh3+ 28.Bxh3 gxh3µ was the game, when White is not yet dead. 28.Nxc2 28.Qxc2 is mated most quickly by 28...Ne2+ (though 28...Nh3+ would get there two moves more slowly). 28.Qxg4 must be met by: 28...Nh3+!–+ Otherwise White is better. 29.Qxh3 Qxf2+ 30.Kh1 Qxe1 White will lose masses of material, then get mated. For example: 31.Rf3 Be4 32.Nxe4 Rxf3 28...Nh3+ 29.Bxh3 Of course 29. Kh1 Nxf2+ is a winning fork. 29...Qxf2+ 30.Kh1 gxh3!–+ When playing 27...Bc2, it was essential to realize this position is winning. The threat of mate on g2 leaves White no time to save the d2-knight. 31.Qg1 Qxd2 Black is only a pawn up, but it’s a forced mate. For example: 32.Ra2 Qe2 Threatening checks on f3 or e4. The Woodpecker Method 379

title: Carlsen – So, Internet (blitz 3.32) 2017
solution: Magnus Carlsen – Wesley So, Internet (blitz 3.32) 2017 24.Rbe1!+– Preparing the queen check on h8 by covering the black king’s escape route. For White, 24.Rbe1 is the right square and the right rook, though you need to see a few key lines to understand why. In the game Carlsen tried to do it all with checks: 24. Qh8+? Ke7 25.Rfe1+ Be6 The position was messy, but had he played 26.Qh4!?² then White would still be a touch better. Instead, the “wrong rook” move 24.Rfe1? allows 24...Be6² when, unlike the main line, White cannot lift the e1-rook, as it would leave its colleague on b1 hanging. 24...Rxe1 24...Be6 is refuted most simply by 25. Re3!+– with the idea Nxe6+ ...fxe6, Rf3 skewering the queen (also winning, but in messier style, is 25.g4+– with the ideas 25... Qxg4+ 26.Qxg4 Bxg4 27.Nh7+! and 25...Qg6 26.f4! threatening f4-f5). 25.Rxe1 Be6 26.Qh8+! Creating an annoying pin on the b8-knight. The second-best 26.f4± secures an advantage, but is too much weaker than the text move to be worthy of any credit. 26...Ke7 27.h4!+– Finding this slow move, defending the knight and creating luft, would be a brilliant achievement for a non- computer. 27.Qxg7 is not such a bad move, but Black can fight on after: 27...Kd6! 28.h4± The obvious 27.Nxe6? throws away all White’s advantage after: 27...fxe6 28.Qxg7+ Kd6= 27...Qd5 T rying to unpin the b8-knight. Unlike the 27.Qxg7 line above, 27... Kd6 no longer works for Black: 28.Nxe6 (or the check on d8 first) 28...fxe6 29.Qd8+ (29.Rd1+ is similar) 29...Kc6 30.Qc8++– Black is busted after 30...Kb6 31.Rxe6+ or 30...Kd6 31.Rd1+ Ke5 32.Qb7 (or many other 32nd moves). 28.Qxg7 28.c4+– also works. For example: 28... Qd4 29.Qh5 Qf6 30.Nxe6 fxe6 31.Qd5 is decisive. 28...Kd8 Or 28...Kd6 can be killed most swiftly by: 29.Nxe6! (the obvious 29.h5 should win, just not at once) 29...fxe6 30.c4!+– For example: 30... Qxc4 31.Qg3+ Ke7 32.Rd1 And the attack wins far too much material. 29.h5+– The h-pawn is going all the way.
